angle: Design A as the base — one unbroken physics-led line from F = ma to Einstein's equations, with every mathematical tool arriving at the exact point a physical problem stalls without it — with five grafts from Design B that fix real holes: a spine unit on perturbation theory and asymptotics (without which Mercury's 43 arcseconds cannot honestly be computed), a spine unit on classical field theory (without which T^μν in Einstein's equation is an incantation), a spine unit on phase-plane analysis (the single best intuition-builder for someone fluent in proof and blank on physics), dimensional analysis and scaling taught explicitly in unit 00 rather than assumed to rub off, and B's slides/problems hour split. Design B's forms-first bet is rejected: teaching flux as a 2-form to a learner who has never computed a flux produces someone who can prove d²=0 and cannot guess which way a field points; forms arrive later, as the unification, in a branch. B's fluids unit is cut and its dimensional-analysis problems harvested. Both designs' express routes were broken — A admitted two substitutions that break closure, B had two unflagged closure bugs — so the dependency graph here is rebuilt so that the express route is genuinely closed: Minkowski space needs only homogeneity, isotropy and mechanics (Maxwell earns the invariant speed, it does not define it), and the field equations have two derivations, the Bianchi–Lovelock–Newtonian-limit route needing only curvature and the equivalence principle. 41 units, 35 spine and 6 branch, ~335 h full and ~195 h express.
premise: **The physics leads and the mathematics follows, and there is no unit called 'Vector Calculus'.** You asked to start directly with mechanics and unit 00 does: Newton's second law read as a differential equation, reduced to quadrature in the three cases where that works. No vector calculus is assumed anywhere, because none is needed until unit 04, where the work integral demands it. Every tool then arrives late and under pressure, with a specific problem already waiting: linear ODE theory with the damped driven oscillator, Frobenius and Bessel with Kepler's equation, Legendre with the Earth's oblateness, the calculus of variations with the brachistochrone, Fourier and Sturm-Liouville with the plucked string and the drum, complex analysis with causality, tensors with the inertia tensor, differential geometry with the failure of flat spacetime to hold gravity. The tensor unit is called 'Rigid bodies' and the PDE unit is called 'the wave equation'. This costs nothing in rigour and buys the one thing that makes self-study of mathematical physics survivable: at every moment you know why you are learning this.

**You have the maturity, so nothing is drilled, everything load-bearing is proved, and nothing is mimed.** The course will not re-explain a limit, a linear map or an inner product. It will prove Picard-Lindelof in unit 01, because determinism is a theorem and not a slogan; prove the Euler-Lagrange equations are coordinate-invariant in unit 12, because that single fact is the seed of general covariance; prove Cauchy's tetrahedron theorem in unit 22, because it is the only place in classical physics where you *prove* rather than assume that a physical quantity is bilinear; prove Noether in unit 13 so that unit 36's Killing vectors are recognisably the same theorem; and prove the Levi-Civita connection unique in unit 32 so the Christoffel symbols are derived rather than posited. Where a proof is a research monograph — KAM, completeness of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions, Lovelock, the singularity theorems — the statement is given precisely, the hypotheses are made explicit, and the proof is cited, never gestured at.

**The three ways a mathematically strong beginner fails at physics are designed against explicitly.** They are: no dimensional sense, no feel for approximation, and no picture of a system they cannot solve. So unit 00 teaches the Buckingham pi theorem and makes you predict the pendulum's period up to a function of one dimensionless group before touching an integral; unit 21 is a full spine unit on asymptotics — optimal truncation, secular terms, boundary layers, Poincare-Lindstedt — and it is the unit that sets up Mercury's precession as a secular term you deliberately do not remove; and unit 02 is a spine unit on phase portraits, Lyapunov functions and bifurcations, which feeds almost nothing downstream and stays on the spine anyway, because it is where a mathematician first *sees* a mechanical system rather than solving one. The reinforcement is numerical: almost every checkpoint ends in a quantity the world can refute. 32.7 h for the Foucault pendulum at the Pantheon, 98.6 degrees for a sun-synchronous orbit at 800 km, 343 m/s for sound in air and 280 for Newton's wrong answer, 2.46e-15 for Pound-Rebka, 42.98 arcseconds per century for Mercury. A derivation with the right structure and the wrong number has not finished.

**It is a dependency graph and it is nearly a chain — and the express route is genuinely closed, which the two drafts this was built from were not.** Unlike your optimization course there are no three independent trunks here; each tool is genuinely load-bearing for the next piece of physics, and saying so is more honest than faking parallelism. What independence exists sits in six branch units (15, 17, 34, 38, 39, 40) and in one real fork: the analytic-and-field line (18-25) and the geometric line both descend from unit 12 and rejoin at unit 28, which needs 27 from one side and 25 from the other. The graph was then built so that a short path to general relativity is a *subgraph* rather than a set of apologies: unit 26 derives the Lorentz group from homogeneity, isotropy and one invariant speed, with Maxwell (unit 25) earning that speed's value rather than defining it; and unit 35 gives two derivations of the field equations, the Bianchi-plus-Lovelock-plus-Newtonian-limit route needing only curvature and the equivalence principle. The express route is therefore 24 units with every need satisfied on the route, and what it costs is named rather than hidden.
assumed_prerequisites: Mathematical maturity: you read and write proofs, you are comfortable with abstraction, quantifiers, epsilon-delta arguments and 'suppose not', and you habitually ask which hypothesis a theorem actually needs. Assumed everywhere; it is the reason the course can move this fast.

Linear algebra, properly: vector spaces, bases, linear maps, dual spaces, determinants, eigenvalues, inner products, the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices, Jordan normal form (stated, used in 06), quadratic forms and their signature, Sylvester's law of inertia. Units 07, 16, 26 and 31 cash this in hard.

Single-variable calculus and real analysis: limits, continuity, uniform convergence, differentiation, the Riemann integral, integration by parts and substitution, Taylor's theorem with remainder, power series and radius of convergence.

Point-set topology of metric spaces: open sets, compactness, completeness, and the Banach fixed-point theorem — used in the first proof of the course (unit 01) and again in unit 04's inverse function theorem.

Elementary group theory: groups, homomorphisms, group actions. Used lightly for SO(3) in 16, one-parameter symmetry groups in 13, and the Lorentz group in 26. No representation theory assumed or taught.

Comfort with a computer algebra system or numerical environment. Nothing is built in this course, but units 09, 17, 19, 21, 37 and 39 have problems whose last step is arithmetic you should not do by hand.

NOT assumed, and all taught here: any physics whatsoever; dimensional analysis; multivariable and vector calculus; ODE solution methods; qualitative ODE theory; Fourier analysis; complex analysis; PDEs; asymptotics; the calculus of variations; tensors; differential forms; differential geometry. 'Start directly with mechanics' means no pre-physics warm-up, not that any of these may be assumed.

trunks.title: Part A — the equation of motion, and the calculus it forces
trunks.thesis: Newton's second law is a differential equation, and this part is one long answer to 'which equation, and how do you solve it?'. The mathematics arrives in five waves, each pulled in by a problem that stalls without it: dimensional analysis and quadrature for one-dimensional motion, qualitative theory for the equations with no formula, multivariable calculus for motion in space, line and flux integrals for work and gravity, and linear ODE theory plus series solutions for oscillators and orbits. It ends with the Kepler problem solved completely — shape and timetable — and the inclination of a real satellite predicted to within a degree.

trunks.title: Part B — the action, and coordinates ceasing to matter
trunks.thesis: Nothing here says anything Newton did not, and that is the point: it is a change of language whose entire value is what it makes obvious. Extremising an integral gives the equations of motion; those equations are then invariant under any change of coordinates, which is the idea that ends the course as general covariance. Symmetry becomes conservation by one theorem. And the part quietly builds the two objects relativity needs — an action principle, and a real definition of a tensor, arriving with the inertia tensor because that is the first place nine numbers per basis will not do.

trunks.title: Part C — the analytic toolkit, fields, and the crisis that ends Newtonian physics
trunks.thesis: Take a chain of oscillators to the continuum and you get a partial differential equation, a field, and the need for four more pieces of mathematics: Fourier and Sturm-Liouville theory, the Fourier transform with the complex analysis that makes it usable, asymptotics for the problems with no exact answer, and tensor fields on space. Electromagnetism is here at full strength and on purpose: it is the only place vector calculus reaches its final form, it is the historical and logical road to relativity, and F_{mu nu} is the canonical tensor field that makes the Riemann tensor's index work familiar rather than alarming. The part ends by showing, with the chain rule and nothing else, that Maxwell's equations do not survive a Galilean boost — and by finding which transformation they do survive.

trunks.title: Part D — Minkowski: relativity as the geometry of a quadratic form, and fields on it
trunks.thesis: Special relativity is presented as the structure it is: a group derived from homogeneity, isotropy and one invariant speed, acting on a vector space carrying an indefinite bilinear form. Every paradox dissolves into a statement about that form — the twin paradox is the reversed triangle inequality — and every dynamical result follows from the free action being proper time. Electromagnetism is then recognised as having been relativistic all along, field theory supplies an honest definition of the stress-energy tensor, and the part closes by taking the equivalence principle seriously and showing, from inside flat spacetime, exactly which feature of gravity Minkowski space cannot represent.

trunks.title: Part E — curved space: the mathematics of 'there is no global inertial frame'
trunks.thesis: The one place in the course where three consecutive units are mathematics first. That is not a lapse in the just-in-time principle but its consequence: unit 30 ends by proving tidal forces cannot be transformed away, and the only honest response is to build the machinery that measures exactly that. Manifolds so that coordinates stop being data, connections so that differentiating a vector field means something, curvature so that the thing no coordinate change removes has a name. The payoff is immediate and precise: geodesic deviation set beside the Newtonian tidal tensor of unit 05, term for term.

trunks.title: Part F — Einstein: the field equations and what they predict
trunks.thesis: Two derivations of the field equations — vary the Einstein-Hilbert action, or observe with Lovelock that nothing else was ever available — then one exact solution and three numbers. The endpoint is not the equation but the arcseconds: Mercury's 43, the factor of two in light deflection that separates Einstein from a Newtonian corpuscle, and the Shapiro delay. Three branches extend the reach — waves, cosmology, rotating holes — and the last names precisely where this course's methods stop.

units.title: Newton's second law is an ODE — and dimensions tell you the answer's shape before you solve it
units.physics: The three laws and what each actually asserts — the first is the definition of an inertial frame, not a special case of the second. Mass, momentum and force laws as constitutive input rather than theorem. One-dimensional motion under constant gravity, linear drag and quadratic drag; terminal velocity. Energy as a first integral; turning points, bounded and unbounded motion, equilibria read off V. Units, dimensions, and the habit this course will not let you drop: write the answer's dimensional form before you integrate anything.
units.math_tools: Second-order ODEs reducible to quadrature in exactly three cases: F(t), integrate twice; F(v), separable in v then invert; F(x), multiply by x-dot and integrate, which is where energy comes from. Separation of variables, implicit solutions, inverting t(x) and recognising when you cannot. Improper integrals at a turning point and when the singularity is integrable. The Buckingham pi theorem, stated and proved as a rank argument on the dimension matrix; similarity and scaling solutions. Elliptic integrals of the first kind named, not developed.
units.worked_example: The plane pendulum, done twice on one slide. First dimensionally: the only groups available are T sqrt(g/l) and the amplitude, so T = sqrt(l/g) f(theta_0) with no mass dependence — two lines, no calculus, and everything except f is already settled. Then exactly: first-integrate theta'' = -(g/l) sin theta, reduce to T = 4 sqrt(l/g) K(sin(theta_0/2)), expand to T ≈ 2 pi sqrt(l/g)(1 + theta_0^2/16 + ...), and find the amplitude at which the small-angle formula is 1 per cent wrong (about 23 degrees). The calculus determined f and nothing else.
units.problem_set: Reduction to quadrature in all three cases with the trap in each, and dimensional arguments carried to a number. "Taylor's blast wave": from E, rho and t alone derive R(t) = C (E t^2/rho)^{1/5}, read the fireball radius off the declassified Trinity photographs' scale bar, and recover a yield near 21 kilotons — a classified number obtained from dimensions and a photograph. "Period by quadrature": for V = k|x|^n derive T proportional to E^{1/n - 1/2}, evaluate the constant as a Beta function, and identify the unique n for which the period is amplitude-independent.
units.checkpoint: Given any force of the form F(t), F(v) or F(x) you first write the answer's dimensional form and name the dimensionless group the calculus is left to determine, then reduce to quadrature and produce the explicit solution or the period integral — and you can classify which of the three forms a problem is in before starting it.

units.title: Determinism, and the one hypothesis it rests on
units.physics: What 'Newton's laws determine the future' means as a mathematical claim. Norton's dome: a mass on a dome shaped so it can spontaneously start moving after an arbitrary delay, with no force applied and no hypothesis violated. Finite-time blow-up: an inverse-cube attractor reaching the origin in finite time, and what that does to global determinism.
units.math_tools: The phase-space reformulation: any m x'' = F(x, x', t) is a first-order system y' = f(y,t) on R^{2n}. Picard-Lindelof proved via the Banach fixed-point theorem on C^0 with a weighted sup norm, with the Lipschitz condition doing all the work. Gronwall's inequality and continuous dependence on initial data. Peano: existence without uniqueness. Maximal intervals of existence and blow-up.
units.worked_example: Norton's dome in full: the surface h(r) = -(2/3g) r^{3/2} gives r'' = sqrt(r); exhibit the one-parameter family r(t) = (t-T)^4/144 for t >= T together with r = 0, verify every member solves the equation with identical initial data, and locate precisely which hypothesis fails — Lipschitz continuity at r = 0, since d/dr sqrt(r) diverges there.
units.problem_set: Verifying the hypotheses where you care and breaking them where you do not. "Prove the pendulum is deterministic": verify local Lipschitz on bounded sets and conclude global existence. "Blow-up": show x' = x^2 escapes in finite time and m x'' = -k/x^3 reaches the origin in finite time, then decide whether either contradicts Picard-Lindelof.
units.checkpoint: You state and prove Picard-Lindelof, and exhibit Norton's dome's one-parameter solution family together with the exact hypothesis that fails — without appealing to physical intuition at any step.

units.title: Phase portraits: what you know when there is no formula
units.physics: The honest position, stated early because everything later depends on accepting it: almost no equation of motion has a closed-form solution, and that is not a gap in the literature. What you get instead is the qualitative picture — how many equilibria, of what type, with which basins, and whether anything periodic exists. The pendulum's separatrix on the cylinder. Damped systems as gradient-like flows; conservative systems as flows preserving a function, which is the first hint of the symplectic structure of unit 14.
units.math_tools: Autonomous systems as vector fields; flows and the one-parameter group property. Equilibria, linearisation, and classification of planar linear systems by trace and determinant. Hartman-Grobman stated, with the sharp fact that it says nothing about centres. Lyapunov's direct method, with LaSalle's invariance principle for the degenerate case. Limit cycles; Poincare-Bendixson, stated with its essential reliance on the plane. The index of a vector field around a closed curve. Bifurcations — saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork, Hopf — with normal forms.
units.worked_example: The damped pendulum theta'' + gamma theta' + sin theta = 0. Draw the full cylinder phase portrait; classify the alternating saddles and spirals; construct V = (1/2) theta'^2 + (1 - cos theta) and use LaSalle to prove asymptotic stability of the down position — a proof linearisation alone cannot give. Then set gamma = 0 and watch the spiral become a centre, which is exactly the case Hartman-Grobman excludes.
units.problem_set: Qualitative analysis where no formula exists, and the traps in linearisation. "When linearisation lies": for x' = -y - x^3, y' = x - y^3 show the linearisation predicts a centre while the origin is asymptotically stable, and give the Lyapunov function that proves it. "Van der Pol has a limit cycle": construct an explicit trapping region and apply Poincare-Bendixson to prove existence without computing the cycle.
units.checkpoint: Given a planar nonlinear system you locate and classify every equilibrium, decide whether linearisation is conclusive at each, construct a Lyapunov function where it is not, and either prove or rule out a periodic orbit using Poincare-Bendixson together with the index theorem.

units.title: Where things are: curves, frames, and the frame that lies to you
units.physics: Motion in three dimensions. Projectile motion with drag. Uniform circular motion and why the acceleration points inward. Rotating reference frames: centrifugal, Coriolis and Euler terms as artefacts of differentiating in a frame that is itself turning. The Foucault pendulum, the eastward deflection of falling bodies, and why cyclones rotate.
units.math_tools: Partial derivatives; the total derivative of a map R^n -> R^m as the linear map best approximating it, and the multivariable chain rule stated once as composition of linear maps rather than as a page of subscripts. Clairaut's theorem with its counterexample. Vector-valued functions of one variable; arc length; the Frenet-Serret frame and the decomposition a = v' T + (v^2/rho) N. Time-dependent orthogonal matrices; antisymmetry of Omega = R^T R' in so(3); the identification of so(3) with R^3 by the cross product; the transport theorem (d/dt)_inertial = (d/dt)_rotating + omega cross.
units.worked_example: Derive the full rotating-frame equation m a_rot = F - 2m omega x v_rot - m omega x (omega x r) - m omega' x r by differentiating x_in = R(t) x_rot twice, then apply it to a pendulum at latitude lambda to get the Foucault precession rate omega sin(lambda) — 32.7 h at the Pantheon's 48.9 N, against the observed roughly 32 h.
units.problem_set: The transport theorem applied until it stops being surprising, plus Frenet computations. "Falling east": compute the eastward Coriolis deflection of a mass dropped 100 m at the equator (about 2.2 cm) and get the sign right. "Circular motion from scratch": show ||v|| constant is equivalent to a dot v = 0 and derive the Frenet decomposition of acceleration from it.
units.checkpoint: Starting only from x_inertial = R(t) x_rotating with R in SO(3) you derive the Coriolis and centrifugal terms, identify omega from R^T R', and predict the Foucault period at a stated latitude to within an hour.

units.title: Work, and the arrival of vector calculus
units.physics: Work as a line integral; the work-energy theorem. Conservative forces and potential energy; energy conservation as a first integral in three dimensions. Why friction and magnetism both fall outside this frame, for opposite reasons. Potential landscapes; equilibrium and stability read off the Hessian.
units.math_tools: Line integrals of vector fields; the gradient and the fundamental theorem of line integrals — with the distinction planted quietly and once: the derivative is a covector and the gradient is what you get after using an inner product to convert it, which is index-raising in unit 26 and nothing else. Green's theorem in the plane and Stokes' theorem in R^3, proved for a rectangle with the patching argument sketched. The curl as the local obstruction to being a gradient; the Poincare lemma on a simply connected domain. Taylor in R^n, the Hessian and classification of nondegenerate critical points; the inverse and implicit function theorems by contraction mapping; Lagrange multipliers derived from the implicit function theorem rather than asserted.
units.worked_example: Show the inverse-square field is conservative by constructing V = -GMm/r along a radial path, then confirm path-independence on a deliberately awkward path. Then the punctured-plane vortex F = (-y, x)/(x^2+y^2): compute curl F = 0 everywhere it is defined and the loop integral 2 pi around the origin, and state exactly what is being measured — the topology of the domain, not the field. The question is left open until unit 34.
units.problem_set: Deciding conservativeness and producing either the potential or the offending loop. "Is it conservative?": five fields, three yes and two no, each requiring V explicitly or a closed loop with nonzero circulation. "Stability": for V(x,y) = x^3 - 3xy^2 classify every critical point by the Hessian and sketch the resulting flow.
units.checkpoint: Given F on an open set U you decide whether it is conservative and defend the answer by producing V explicitly or exhibiting a loop with nonzero circulation — including at least one case where the answer depends on the shape of U rather than on F.

units.title: Flux, Gauss, and gravity stops being a force between pairs
units.physics: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the shell theorem, which cost Newton years. The gravitational field as an object in its own right; the field equation div g = -4 pi G rho, equivalently Laplacian Phi = 4 pi G rho. Tidal forces as the variation of the field across a body, and the tidal tensor d_i d_j Phi, trace-free in vacuum. Why the Moon raises two bulges and not one.
units.math_tools: Multiple integrals and Fubini; change of variables and the Jacobian; spherical and cylindrical coordinates, with the coordinate singularities identified. Surface integrals and flux. The divergence theorem, proved for a box with patching sketched. The Laplacian and harmonic functions; the mean-value property and the maximum principle. Solid angle, and why 1/r^2 is the unique power in three dimensions for which flux is radius-independent.
units.worked_example: Prove the shell theorem twice: by brute integration over the sphere with the law of cosines, where the punchline hides in an algebraic cancellation, then by Gauss's flux law plus symmetry in three lines. Then compute Phi inside a uniform sphere and show a body dropped down a tunnel through the Earth executes simple harmonic motion with period 84.5 min, independent of where the tunnel's ends are.
units.problem_set: Flux arguments where symmetry does the work, and the tidal tensor. "The trace-free tidal tensor": compute d_i d_j Phi for a point mass, show the trace vanishes and the eigenvalues are (-2, 1, 1) GM/r^3, and deduce the two tidal bulges from the eigenvectors — this object is the Newtonian limit of the Riemann tensor and unit 33 will say so. "Where Gauss fails": a non-symmetric distribution for which Gauss's law is true but useless, with a precise statement of what symmetry buys.
units.checkpoint: You prove the shell theorem by Gauss's law in under half a page, and compute the tidal tensor of a point mass, showing it is trace-free and reading its two bulges off its eigenvectors.

units.title: The damped driven oscillator, which is most of linear physics
units.physics: Small oscillations about a stable equilibrium as the universal local model: Taylor-expand any V at a minimum and the leading term is (1/2) k x^2. Damping regimes and the quality factor Q. Sinusoidal driving; resonance, the phase lag sweeping through it, the half-power width. The impulse response, and the claim that a linear system's response to everything is its response to one thing. Causality as a constraint on the response function — stated here, cashed at unit 20.
units.math_tools: C and the complex exponential as computational infrastructure — algebra, not yet analysis. Linear ODEs with constant coefficients: characteristic polynomial, the solution space as a two-dimensional vector space (Picard-Lindelof from unit 01, not folklore), the Wronskian and Abel's identity, superposition, variation of parameters, resonance as the failure of the particular-solution ansatz. The Green's function of L = d^2/dt^2 + gamma d/dt + omega_0^2, built by matching a jump in the derivative across t = t': G(t) = exp(-gamma t/2) sin(omega_d t)/omega_d for t > 0 and 0 otherwise. Convolution and Duhamel's principle.
units.worked_example: Solve x'' + gamma x' + omega_0^2 x = F_0 cos(omega t) completely: amplitude F_0/sqrt((omega_0^2-omega^2)^2 + gamma^2 omega^2), phase lag sweeping 0 to pi, peak at omega_0 sqrt(1 - gamma^2/2 omega_0^2), full width at half power gamma. Then build G(t) from its defining property and recover the identical steady state by convolution — the same answer twice by unrelated machinery.
units.problem_set: Building and using Green's functions; regime classification. "Square-pulse drive": solve by convolution with G and separately by matching piecewise solutions at the pulse edges, and confirm they agree including at the corners. "Resonance is not at omega_0": show the amplitude response peaks at sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2 gamma^2) while the velocity response peaks exactly at omega_0, and say which a physicist means. "Critical damping is genuinely special": show gamma = 2 omega_0 gives the Jordan-block degeneracy t exp(-gamma t/2), and that it is the fastest return without overshoot.
units.checkpoint: You construct G(t - t') from its defining property, solve an arbitrary drive by convolution, verify against a directly computed piecewise solution, and can say why the solution space is two-dimensional by citing unit 01.

units.title: Many oscillators, and the spectral theorem earning its keep
units.physics: Two masses and three springs; beats as interference between two normal modes. Normal modes and normal coordinates: the change of basis in which a coupled system becomes n uncoupled oscillators. N masses in a line with fixed ends. Zero modes and the symmetries responsible for them. Why a system with n coordinates has exactly n modes.
units.math_tools: Linear systems x' = Ax; the matrix exponential; the general solution from eigendecomposition and the Jordan form for the degenerate case. The generalised eigenvalue problem K v = omega^2 M v with M symmetric positive definite: reduce by M^{1/2} to a symmetric problem, hence real omega^2 and M-orthogonal modes — the spectral theorem doing physical work, and the reason the naive 'diagonalise both' is false in general. Simultaneous diagonalisation of two quadratic forms when one is definite, with the counterexample when neither is. The Rayleigh quotient and the variational characterisation of the lowest frequency.
units.worked_example: N equal masses and N+1 equal springs between fixed walls: write M and K, try v_j = sin(j k pi/(N+1)), verify, and obtain exactly omega_k = 2 sqrt(k/m) sin(k pi/2(N+1)). Plot omega_k against k for N = 20 and watch the curve bend away from the straight line. That bending is dispersion; the straight part is the sound wave unit 18 recovers in the continuum limit, and the leading correction -(ck)(ka)^2/24 is a rare chance to see a continuum theory's own error bar.
units.problem_set: Modes of small systems and the M-inner product. "Beats": for two masses and three springs compute both modes and show displacing one mass alone makes energy slosh at the difference frequency. "Orthogonality by hand": for a chain with one heavy mass verify v_i^T M v_j = 0 numerically, show naive Euclidean orthogonality fails, and explain which inner product was right all along. "Rayleigh bounds a frequency": bound the lowest mode of a five-mass chain with a trial vector and compare with the exact answer.
units.checkpoint: For any (M, K) with M symmetric positive definite you produce the normal frequencies and mode shapes, verify orthogonality in the M-inner product rather than the Euclidean one, identify every zero mode with the symmetry responsible, and can explain why complex frequencies cannot occur.

units.title: The central-force problem, and the two conservation laws that solve it
units.physics: Torque and angular momentum; conservation for central forces and the immediate consequence that motion is planar. The two-body problem reduced to one body of reduced mass mu. The effective potential V_eff = V(r) + L^2/2 mu r^2, from whose graph the entire qualitative theory of orbits can be read — bound, unbound, circular, and the centrifugal barrier. Kepler's three laws derived rather than quoted. The Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector, and the fact that it is *extra*: most central forces have nothing like it.
units.math_tools: The cross product and its identities. Conserved quantities as first integrals lowering the order of an ODE system, six to two here. Quadrature for r(t) and theta(r). The Binet substitution u = 1/r, turning the orbit into u'' + u = -(mu/L^2 u^2) F(1/u) — linear for the inverse-square law, and the single most useful change of variable in the course, since unit 37 adds exactly one term to it and gets general relativity. Bertrand's theorem cited; its computational half is a problem.
units.worked_example: The Kepler problem end to end: from F = -k/r^2 obtain u'' + u = mu k/L^2, hence r = p/(1 + e cos theta) with p = L^2/mu k and e = sqrt(1 + 2 E L^2/mu k^2); classify by e and show e < 1 iff E < 0; derive T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/GM from the areal velocity. Then A = p x L - mu k r-hat: verify dA/dt = 0 by direct differentiation and read the orbit equation off A dot r in one line.
units.problem_set: Effective potentials, stability of circular orbits, and closure. "Which power laws close?": show circular orbits of F proportional to r^n are stable for n > -3, that small radial oscillations have frequency omega_theta sqrt(3+n), and hence that orbits close only for n = -2 and n = 1. "Escape and deflection": compute escape speed, then the hyperbolic deflection angle for a given impact parameter, obtaining Rutherford's formula.
units.checkpoint: From V(r) = -k/r alone you derive r(theta) = p/(1 + e cos theta), express e and p in terms of E and L, prove Kepler's second and third laws, and verify the Runge-Lenz vector is conserved by explicit differentiation.

units.title: Where is the planet at time t? Kepler's equation and the birth of Bessel functions
units.physics: The orbit's shape was easy; its timetable is not. The eccentric anomaly; Kepler's equation E - e sin E = M, transcendental and with no closed-form inverse — the problem that occupied celestial mechanics for two centuries and that every ephemeris still solves.
units.math_tools: Solution by series in a parameter. The Fourier-Bessel expansion E = M + 2 sum_n J_n(ne) sin(nM)/n, which is where Bessel functions were actually born. Bessel's equation x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - n^2) y = 0; the Frobenius method at a regular singular point; the indicial equation, the two roots, and the logarithmic second solution when they differ by an integer. Recurrence relations, the generating function exp((x/2)(t - 1/t)), Bessel's integral representation, and the asymptotic sqrt(2/pi x) cos(x - n pi/2 - pi/4). Lagrange inversion as the general mechanism. The Laplace limit e = 0.6627434..., asserted here and proved in unit 20 — a debt deliberately incurred.
units.worked_example: Derive the Bessel series for E(M) by computing the Fourier coefficients of E - M and recognising Bessel's integral representation. Then locate Mars (e = 0.0934) at a stated epoch to five significant figures using three terms, and cross-check against Newton's method applied directly to the transcendental equation, counting the iterations each route costs.
units.problem_set: Frobenius practice and honest convergence. "Frobenius by hand": solve Bessel's equation of order zero by series, exhibit the logarithmic second solution, and observe that the method detects the obstruction on its own rather than being told about it. "Halley's comet": with e = 0.967, past the Laplace limit, show the series fails numerically and locate empirically where it begins to diverge.
units.checkpoint: You derive the Bessel-function solution of Kepler's equation from its Fourier coefficients and use it to place a planet to five digits — and you can state exactly where it diverges while owing unit 20 the reason.

units.title: Real planets are not points: multipoles, Legendre, and secular perturbation
units.physics: The potential of a non-spherical body. The Earth's oblateness and its J2 = 1.0826e-3, the largest non-spherical term in the solar system by effect. Its consequence: a satellite's orbital plane precesses, which is exploited rather than fought. Tides revisited as the l = 2 term; why the Moon is tidally locked.
units.math_tools: The generating function (1 - 2xt + t^2)^{-1/2} = sum P_n(x) t^n defining the Legendre polynomials; Legendre's equation and its polynomial solutions; Rodrigues' formula; orthogonality on [-1,1]. The multipole expansion of 1/|r - r'| with monopole, dipole and quadrupole terms and their coordinate-independent meanings. First-order perturbation theory for ODEs: osculating orbital elements, the method of averaging, and the distinction between secular and periodic terms — the first appearance of the idea unit 21 develops properly and unit 37 spends.
units.worked_example: Expand Phi for an axially symmetric body, identify J2 with the quadrupole moment, and derive the nodal precession rate Omega-dot = -(3/2) J2 (R_E/a)^2 n cos(i)/(1-e^2)^2. Then solve Omega-dot = 360 degrees per year for a circular orbit at 800 km altitude and obtain i = 98.6 degrees — the actual inclination of every sun-synchronous satellite ever flown.
units.problem_set: Multipole computations and secular perturbation. "Quadrupole of an ellipsoid": compute J2 for an oblate spheroid of given flattening and check the Earth's value against f = 1/298.257. "Apsidal precession": show the J2 term also precesses perigee, compute the rate, and find the critical inclination 63.4 degrees at which it vanishes — which is why Molniya orbits use exactly that.
units.checkpoint: From J2 alone you predict the sun-synchronous inclination at a stated altitude to within a degree of the published value, and you can say which Legendre term produces each of the two precessions.

units.title: The brachistochrone, and how to differentiate with respect to a curve
units.physics: Johann Bernoulli's 1696 challenge. Fermat's principle of least time, with Snell's law falling out of it. The hanging chain. The common structure: nature appears to extremise an integral, and the question is what equation that forces.
units.math_tools: Functionals on spaces of curves; admissible variations and the first variation as a Gateaux derivative. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations and the du Bois-Reymond form you actually need, both proved with bump functions. The Euler-Lagrange equation. The Beltrami identity when the integrand lacks explicit dependence on the independent variable. Natural boundary conditions at a free endpoint. Isoperimetric and holonomic constraints by Lagrange multipliers in function space. Several dependent variables; higher derivatives. The second variation, the Legendre condition, the accessory equation and Jacobi's conjugate points — because 'stationary action' is not 'least action' and unit 26 will need to know which. The direct method, and Weierstrass's demolition of Dirichlet's principle as the reason existence is a real question.
units.worked_example: The brachistochrone in full: set up T[y] = integral sqrt((1+y'^2)/2gy) dx, apply Beltrami, integrate to the cycloid in parametric form, fix both constants from the endpoints, and confirm with explicit numbers that it beats the straight line and the circular arc. Then the catenary by the same route with the length constraint handled by a multiplier, noting the multiplier is physically the tension, and finish with a conjugate-point check that the cycloid really is a minimum.
units.problem_set: Deriving Euler-Lagrange equations and probing their limits. "Snell from Fermat": derive refraction, then its continuous version for a medium with n(y), and solve the ray path in a linear gradient — a mirage, with a number. "Stationary but not minimal": exhibit a great-circle arc exceeding half the circle, show it fails the Jacobi condition, and identify the conjugate point as the antipode. "Geodesics on a surface of revolution": derive them and obtain Clairaut's relation r sin psi = const as a first integral, which unit 36 re-derives as a Killing vector.
units.checkpoint: You derive the cycloid from scratch, and you produce a functional whose Euler-Lagrange solution is stationary but not a minimum, together with the test — conjugate point or second variation — that detects it.

units.title: Lagrangian mechanics: coordinates stop mattering
units.physics: Hamilton's principle with L = T - V. D'Alembert's principle and virtual work. Generalised coordinates; holonomic constraints eliminated by choosing coordinates rather than by computing constraint forces. The double pendulum. The bead on a rotating hoop and its bifurcation. Constraint forces recovered when wanted, via multipliers. Gauge freedom L -> L + df/dt. Velocity-dependent potentials, with the Lagrangian for a charge in an electromagnetic field written down now and justified in unit 24. Non-holonomic constraints, with an honest statement that their variational treatment is subtle and often done wrong.
units.math_tools: Proof that the Euler-Lagrange equations of L = T - V are equivalent to Newton's equations in Cartesian coordinates. Proof of the central fact: they are form-invariant under any invertible change of coordinates q -> Q(q,t) — the reason the formalism exists, and the first appearance of the idea that ends the course as general covariance. Generalised momenta and cyclic coordinates. Linearisation about equilibria, reconnecting with unit 07's generalised eigenvalue machinery unchanged. Configuration space as a manifold, informally here and precisely in unit 31.
units.worked_example: The bead on a hoop rotating at Omega: derive L, read off V_eff, and find the pitchfork bifurcation at Omega^2 = g/R where the bottom of the hoop goes unstable and two equilibria appear at cos(theta) = g/R Omega^2 — three lines, against the page it takes from a force balance, and unit 02's normal form recognisable in it. Draw the phase portrait on each side. Then the double pendulum's L and its linearised normal modes.
units.problem_set: Writing Lagrangians and exploiting invariance. "Same system, two coordinate systems": treat a spherical pendulum in (theta, phi) and again in Cartesian coordinates with a multiplier, and show the motions agree. "Gauge freedom is real": show L and L + df/dt give identical equations but different canonical momenta, and identify which physical quantity is therefore not gauge-invariant. "Atwood's machine with an elastic string": three degrees of freedom, and the point is that you never draw a free-body diagram or name a tension.
units.checkpoint: You write L for one system in two genuinely different coordinate systems, derive both sets of Euler-Lagrange equations, show they describe the same motion, and state the theorem that guaranteed this in advance.

units.title: Noether: every conservation law you have met is one theorem
units.physics: Momentum conservation is spatial homogeneity, angular momentum is isotropy, energy is invariance under time translation. The Galilean boost and its less familiar conserved charge. The Runge-Lenz vector of unit 08 finally explained as the charge of a symmetry that is not a symmetry of space at all — the hidden SO(4) of the Kepler problem. What the theorem does not say: the converse is false.
units.math_tools: One-parameter groups of transformations of configuration space and the induced variation of the action; the infinitesimal generator. Statement and complete proof of Noether's theorem for point mechanics — three lines, which this learner will appreciate seeing — including the quasi-invariant case where L changes by a total time derivative. Why the energy function h = sum q'_i dL/dq'_i - L is the conserved quantity, and equals T + V only when the constraints are time-independent: a distinction almost universally glossed over, and one this course needs later.
units.worked_example: Prove Noether's theorem in full generality, then run it four times on the Kepler Lagrangian: time translation gives energy, rotation gives all three components of angular momentum, the Galilean boost q -> q + vt is quasi-invariant and gives G = pt - mq (the centre of mass moving uniformly, restated as a conservation law), and the SO(4) generator gives the Runge-Lenz vector.
units.problem_set: Finding symmetries and their charges, including hidden ones and one careful counterexample. "Energy is not always T+V": unit 12's bead on the rotating hoop has a conserved h that is not the energy, and the motor driving the hoop does work — compute both and reconcile them. "Scaling symmetry of Kepler": show (t, r) -> (lambda^3 t, lambda^2 r) maps solutions to solutions and recognise Kepler's third law falling out of the resulting charge. "The converse fails": exhibit a conserved quantity arising from no point symmetry, and say what enlargement to phase space (unit 14) would rescue it.
units.checkpoint: Given any Lagrangian and any one-parameter symmetry you write the conserved quantity and verify it is constant on-shell — including one quasi-invariant case where L itself is not invariant and the charge acquires the extra term.

units.title: Hamilton: phase space, and flows that preserve volume
units.physics: The phase-space picture and what it makes visible that configuration space hides: the pendulum's separatrix from unit 02 now as a level set of H, the structure of the Kepler problem, and the fact that trajectories never cross. Liouville's theorem and its meaning — a cloud of initial conditions deforms without shrinking, which is why statistical mechanics is possible and why integrators for mechanics should be symplectic.
units.math_tools: The Legendre transform done properly as convex duality: definition by supremum, involutivity for convex functions, the degenerate case flagged in advance (unit 27's relativistic free particle is nearly one), and the relation to Young's inequality. Hamilton's equations as a first-order system on R^{2n}. Poisson brackets with bilinearity, antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity; {., H} generates time evolution, so conserved quantities are exactly those commuting with H — Noether's converse, now cheap. Canonical transformations and the four generating functions. Liouville's theorem as divergence-freeness of the Hamiltonian vector field. The symplectic form omega = dp wedge dq named here and unpacked in unit 34.
units.worked_example: Legendre-transform the Lagrangians of units 12 and 08, then sketch the Kepler phase portrait in (r, p_r) at fixed L, identifying the separatrix at E = 0. Then compute {L_i, L_j} = epsilon_ijk L_k, and {L_i, A_j} and {A_i, A_j} for the Runge-Lenz vector, watching the algebra close on so(4) for bound orbits and so(3,1) for unbound ones — which is what 'hidden symmetry' meant in unit 13.
units.problem_set: Canonicity tests and bracket algebra. "Is it canonical?": test a given transformation three ways — the symplectic condition M^T J M = J, preservation of all Poisson brackets, and an explicit generating function — and confirm the verdicts agree. "Liouville by hand": follow a rectangle of initial conditions through the free-particle and harmonic-oscillator flows, compute the area at time t, and watch the shear do all the work.
units.checkpoint: You prove a given transformation canonical by two independent routes, perform a Legendre transform including its degenerate case, and prove Liouville's theorem from Hamilton's equations in three lines.

units.title: Hamilton-Jacobi: mechanics was optics all along, and free motion is already geodesic motion
units.physics: Action as a function of its endpoints; solving a mechanical problem by solving one PDE and then differentiating. Action-angle variables: the frequencies of a bounded motion without ever solving for the motion. Adiabatic invariants via the slowly shortened pendulum. Then the two payoffs that make this the course's quiet centre. The optical-mechanical analogy — Fermat against Maupertuis, wavefronts against surfaces of constant S, rays against trajectories. And the Jacobi metric: a particle of energy E in a potential V moves on a *geodesic* of the conformally rescaled metric 2(E - V) delta_ij. Free motion is geodesic motion, in Newtonian physics, before any curvature exists. This is the branch that makes unit 32 feel inevitable rather than imposed, and the one I would fight hardest to keep.
units.math_tools: The Hamilton-Jacobi equation dS/dt + H(q, dS/dq, t) = 0, the course's first nonlinear first-order PDE. Complete integrals versus general solutions; Jacobi's theorem proved in the verification direction, which needs only the chain rule. Separability and Staeckel's conditions, stated. Action variables I_i as loop integrals of p dq over topological cycles, and the conjugate angles. The eikonal limit. Conformal rescaling of a metric.
units.worked_example: Solve the Kepler problem by Hamilton-Jacobi separation in spherical coordinates: write S = -Et + L_z phi + Theta(theta) + R(r), separate, and read the orbit off dS/d(alpha) = constant without integrating an equation of motion. Compute the action variables, obtain H = -mk^2/2I^2 and hence the Kepler frequency by differentiation — and note that all three frequencies being degenerate is exactly why Kepler orbits close, which is Bertrand's theorem seen from above. Then write the Jacobi metric for the same problem and exhibit Kepler orbits as its geodesics.
units.problem_set: Separation, invariants, and frequencies without trajectories. "Frequency without motion": for V = (1/2)k x^2 + lambda x^4 compute I(E) to first order in lambda, obtain the amplitude-dependent frequency shift, and check it against unit 21's Poincare-Lindstedt answer. "Adiabatic invariance": show I is conserved for a pendulum shortened slowly, compute the work done pulling the string through a hole, and confirm the two answers agree.
units.checkpoint: You solve a separable Hamilton-Jacobi problem, extract action-angle variables, produce the oscillation frequency of an anharmonic oscillator without ever integrating its equation of motion, and write the Jacobi metric for a given V and E.

units.title: Rigid bodies, and what a tensor actually is
units.physics: Rigid-body kinematics; the configuration space SO(3) x R^3. Angular momentum L = I omega, and the fact that L is generally not parallel to omega, which is the whole subject. Principal axes; the parallel-axis theorem; Euler's equations in the body frame; the free symmetric top and its two cones; the gyroscope; the intermediate-axis (tennis-racket) theorem. Euler angles and their coordinate singularities, which unit 31 will explain are a fact about SO(3) and not about carelessness.
units.math_tools: Multilinear maps as the definition of a tensor: a (0,2)-tensor is a bilinear map V x V -> R, and the transformation law is a consequence of a change of basis rather than a definition. (p,q)-tensors, tensor products, contraction, symmetric and antisymmetric parts. The dual space and why it is not canonically V — the covector-versus-gradient point planted in unit 04, now made structural, so that units 28 through 35 can raise and lower honestly. Index notation and the Einstein summation convention introduced properly. The spectral theorem producing principal axes. SO(3), so(3), and the exponential map.
units.worked_example: Compute the inertia tensor of a uniform rectangular block about a corner, diagonalise it, verify the transformation law I' = R I R^T component by component under a 45-degree rotation, then linearise Euler's equations about each principal axis and prove the intermediate axis unstable with growth rate sqrt((I_2 - I_1)(I_3 - I_2)) omega / sqrt(I_1 I_3) — a prediction testable with a book and a rubber band, and checkable against the Dzhanibekov footage's flip period.
units.problem_set: Tensor computations and rotational dynamics. "The transformation law is a theorem": compute I in two frames and verify I' = R I R^T, then exhibit a collection of nine numbers per basis that is not a tensor and say precisely what it fails. "The gyroscope": derive the steady precession rate of a heavy symmetric top and the nutation superposed on it, and identify which approximation the elementary torque-equals-dL/dt argument silently makes.
units.checkpoint: For an explicitly given body you compute I in two frames, verify the transformation law component by component, predict which axis is unstable, and can explain in one sentence why nine numbers per basis is not enough to be a tensor.

units.title: Integrability and chaos: determinism without predictability
units.physics: The three-body problem and what Poincare found in it, including the error in the prize memoir. Sensitive dependence; the double pendulum. Integrable systems as the exception rather than the rule: Liouville-Arnold tori. KAM as the statement that most tori survive small perturbation, and that the ones that do not are exactly the resonant ones. Resonances and the Kirkwood gaps in the asteroid belt, an observable consequence with a number attached. What this implies for the stability of the solar system.
units.math_tools: Complete integrability; the Liouville-Arnold theorem with hypotheses and the geometry of its proof. Poincare sections and return maps; area-preserving maps; the standard map; Chirikov's overlap criterion. Lyapunov exponents defined via the linearised flow, with Oseledets cited. KAM stated with its Diophantine condition and an honest account of what 'small' means. Melnikov's method stated. And the contrast with unit 01: solutions are unique and depend continuously on data, which is entirely compatible with being useless for prediction, because continuous dependence is not uniform in t.
units.worked_example: Henon-Heiles, computed. Integrate at four energies, plot the Poincare section at each, and watch the invariant curves dissolve into a chaotic sea as E passes 1/8 — the single most convincing picture in classical mechanics. Then compute the largest Lyapunov exponent in the chaotic region and confirm it is positive there and zero on a surviving torus.
units.problem_set: Distinguishing integrable from chaotic with the tools rather than by eye. "Gronwall's revenge": use unit 01's continuous-dependence bound to show error grows at most like exp(Lt), show the rate is achieved, and conclude determinism and unpredictability are consistent rather than in tension. "The last torus": apply Chirikov's criterion to the standard map, then locate the critical kick strength numerically and compare with Greene's 0.9716. "Kirkwood": compute the semi-major axes of the 3:1 and 5:2 Jovian resonances against the observed gaps.
units.checkpoint: You compute a largest Lyapunov exponent for a given map, produce a Poincare section that constitutes evidence for chaos rather than an impression of it, and explain — quoting unit 01's theorem precisely — why a positive exponent does not contradict uniqueness.

units.title: From N masses to a field: the wave equation
units.physics: The loaded string as N goes to infinity with total mass fixed; the wave equation with c = sqrt(T/mu), derived from a force balance on an element with the small-slope approximation stated and its error named. Travelling and standing waves; superposition; reflection at fixed and free ends, with and without inversion. Energy density and flux, and the local conservation law relating them. The string as a Lagrangian system with infinitely many degrees of freedom: the Lagrangian density and the Euler-Lagrange equation for a field, which is the first field theory in the course.
units.math_tools: The continuum limit as a limit of second-difference operators. Classification of second-order linear PDEs by the principal symbol — hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic — reduction to canonical form, and what each class will accept as data. Characteristics; d'Alembert's formula derived by xi = x - ct, eta = x + ct; domain of dependence and range of influence; finite propagation speed as a theorem rather than an assumption. Hadamard well-posedness, with an explicit ill-posed problem to show the classification has teeth. Uniqueness by energy methods.
units.worked_example: Pluck a string at a/L of its length: take the triangular initial profile with zero initial velocity, extend it oddly and periodically to handle the fixed ends, and follow d'Alembert's solution to draw the exact shape at t = L/4c, L/2c and 3L/4c — the flat-topped travelling kinks that high-speed photography of a real string actually shows.
units.problem_set: d'Alembert with boundaries, and classification with consequences. "Reflection": solve for a pulse meeting a fixed end and a free end by images, and get both signs right. "Classify and break": classify u_xx + 2b u_xy + c u_yy = 0 by b^2 - ac, then work through Hadamard's example showing the Cauchy problem for Laplace's equation is ill-posed with data as small as you please. "Tricomi": classify u_yy + y u_xx = 0 and show it changes type across y = 0, which is what makes transonic flow hard.
units.checkpoint: You solve an initial-boundary-value problem for the finite string by images, classify a given second-order PDE and state what data it will accept, and write the Lagrangian density whose Euler-Lagrange equation is the wave equation.

units.title: Fourier and Sturm-Liouville: the modes are a basis, and that is a theorem
units.physics: Separation of variables on the finite string, and the claim that every initial shape is a superposition of its modes. Timbre: why a plucked and a struck string at the same pitch sound different, and why plucking at one seventh of the length silences the seventh harmonic — a prediction you can hear. Then the same pattern in three geometries: the string gives sines, the circular drum gives Bessel functions, the sphere gives Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics. Heat conduction in a rod, which was Fourier's own problem. Why strings are tuneful and drums are not.
units.math_tools: Fourier sine, cosine and complex series; orthogonality; Bessel's inequality; Parseval; completeness in L^2 stated with the Fejer route sketched. Dirichlet's pointwise theorem for piecewise-C^1 functions and convergence to the midpoint at a jump; uniform convergence and its failure; Gibbs' phenomenon with its 8.9490 per cent overshoot computed; the dictionary between smoothness and coefficient decay, which makes truncation error predictable; term-by-term differentiation and exactly what it costs. Then the Sturm-Liouville operator (p u')' + q u = -lambda w u: formal self-adjointness by Lagrange's identity, the boundary conditions that make it genuinely self-adjoint, and each consequence proved — eigenvalues real and simple, eigenfunctions w-orthogonal, spectrum discrete and unbounded. Completeness via compactness of the resolvent, stated. Sturm's oscillation theorem. The Rayleigh quotient and the variational characterisation of eigenvalues, which is unit 11's calculus of variations in its second job. Bessel and Legendre recognised as two instances of one theorem; spherical harmonics from separating the Laplacian.
units.worked_example: The circular drum: separate in polar coordinates, arrive at Bessel's equation, impose regularity at the centre and vanishing at the rim, and obtain frequency ratios 1 : 1.593 : 2.136 : 2.296 — irrational, therefore not a chord, which is why a drum has no pitch. Then bound the fundamental eigenvalue above with a one-parameter trial function via the Rayleigh quotient and compare with the exact first Bessel zero 2.4048.
units.problem_set: Expansions, convergence rates, and proving the Sturm-Liouville properties. "Hear the coefficients": compute b_n proportional to (1/n^2) sin(n pi a/L) for the plucked string, show plucking at a = L/7 makes b_7 vanish, bound the L^2 truncation error by Parseval as N^{-3} against the struck string's N^{-1}, and say which sounds brighter and why. "Self-adjointness does the work": prove reality and orthogonality from Lagrange's identity, then find the boundary condition that breaks it and see which conclusion fails first. "Legendre from separation": put Legendre's equation in Sturm-Liouville form, identify p, q and w, and prove orthogonality without touching a generating function.
units.checkpoint: Given a Sturm-Liouville problem you prove reality and orthogonality from self-adjointness, count the zeros of the third eigenfunction correctly, bound the lowest eigenvalue above to within a few per cent by a trial function, and expand a given initial profile with a correct statement of what kind of convergence you have.

units.title: The Fourier transform, complex analysis, and why causality is a statement about poles
units.physics: The response of a linear system to any input, not only periodic ones; the susceptibility of unit 06's oscillator. Causality — a system cannot respond before it is driven — and the discovery that this innocuous statement constrains the entire frequency response. Dispersion: why glass separates colours, and why refraction and absorption are not independent. Wave packets, phase and group velocity, packet spreading.
units.math_tools: The Fourier transform on R; inversion; Plancherel; the convolution theorem; differentiation becoming multiplication; the uncertainty relation proved by Cauchy-Schwarz. Test functions and distributions, introduced properly and retroactively legitimising unit 06's Green's function. Then complex analysis: holomorphy and Cauchy-Riemann, Goursat and Cauchy's theorem, the integral formula and its consequences (infinitely differentiable, analytic, Liouville, maximum modulus, Morera), Laurent series, isolated singularities, the residue theorem, Jordan's lemma, principal values, branch points and cuts, the argument principle and Rouche, analytic continuation. Contour integration as the tool for inverting transforms, and the Bromwich contour for the Laplace transform. Asymptotics of integrals belongs here and not in unit 21: Watson's lemma, Laplace's method, stationary phase, and steepest descent by contour deformation.
units.worked_example: Invert the susceptibility 1/(omega_0^2 - omega^2 - i gamma omega) by residues: locate both poles, both in the lower half-plane, close upwards for t < 0 to get exactly zero and downwards for t > 0 to collect both residues — recovering precisely the Green's function built by hand in unit 06, now with its step function explained rather than imposed. Then the proved equivalence: G(t) = 0 for t < 0 iff the susceptibility is holomorphic in the upper half-plane iff the Kramers-Kronig relations hold between its real and imaginary parts.
units.problem_set: Contour technique, with the debts of earlier units called in. "The Laplace limit, finally": locate the complex singularity of the inverse of Kepler's equation and prove unit 09's series has radius of convergence 0.6627434..., which unit 09 could only assert. "Kramers-Kronig": derive the dispersion relations from analyticity, verify them on the oscillator, and conclude that a medium which refracts must also absorb. "Fresnel by octant": evaluate the integrals of cos(x^2) and sin(x^2) with an honest arc estimate — the integral stationary phase generalises.
units.checkpoint: You compute a retarded Green's function by contour integration and prove it vanishes for t < 0 by a contour-closing argument rather than by inspection, evaluate a real integral by steepest descent with every arc estimate justified, and settle unit 09's Laplace limit.

units.title: Perturbation theory: the series that diverges and is still right
units.physics: The uncomfortable truth under most quantitative physics: the exact answer is unavailable, the approximate one is a divergent series, and truncated in the right place it is accurate to ten digits. What an asymptotic expansion means, and why convergence is neither necessary nor sufficient for usefulness. Secular terms and why naive perturbation of an oscillator fails after one period. Boundary layers as the generic behaviour when a small parameter multiplies the highest derivative. Nondimensionalisation as the systematic way to find out which terms you are allowed to drop — unit 00's dimensional habit, now in its working form.
units.math_tools: Order notation, asymptotic sequences, Poincare's definition of an asymptotic expansion with the standard example sum n! x^n; optimal truncation and the exponentially small error; Borel summation named. Regular perturbation. Singular perturbation: matched asymptotic expansions, inner and outer solutions, the intermediate variable, Van Dyke's matching rule. Poincare-Lindstedt and multiple scales for removing secular terms. The WKB approximation, its validity condition and turning points, with the connection formulae stated — and the observation that this is unit 15's eikonal again. Integral asymptotics lives in unit 20 and is cited here, not repeated.
units.worked_example: Two calculations, joined. First the Duffing oscillator x'' + x + epsilon x^3 = 0: show naive perturbation produces a secular term t sin t that destroys the approximation after t ~ 1/epsilon, then apply Poincare-Lindstedt to get omega = 1 + 3 epsilon A^2/8 + O(epsilon^2) and check it numerically. Then point the same machinery at its eventual target: set up u'' + u = GM/L^2 + epsilon u^2 and show that here the secular term is *not* to be removed — it is the perihelion precession, and it is real. The calculation is completed in unit 37, and this is the unit that makes it honest rather than a conjuring trick.
units.problem_set: Getting numbers out of expansions and knowing when to stop. "Optimal truncation": for the Stieltjes series sum (-1)^n n! x^n at x = 0.1 find the smallest term, truncate there, compare with the exact integral value, and confirm the error is the size of the first omitted term. "A boundary layer": solve epsilon y'' + y' + y = 0 on [0,1] with y(0)=0, y(1)=1 by matched asymptotics, locate the layer, and compare the composite approximation with the exact solution at epsilon = 0.01. "Kolmogorov by dimensions alone": from the dissipation rate and the wavenumber derive E(k) proportional to epsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3} and the Kolmogorov length, and check the exponent against published wind-tunnel spectra.
units.checkpoint: Given a perturbed problem you nondimensionalise it, tell regular from singular, remove secular terms by Poincare-Lindstedt or multiple scales, construct and match a boundary layer, and for a divergent asymptotic series find the optimal truncation point and state the accuracy it achieves — and you can say, for the relativistic orbit equation, why the secular term must be kept.

units.title: Continuum mechanics: the stress tensor, and conservation laws in local form
units.physics: A deformable body, for which 'the force on it' is not a single vector. Cauchy's stress tensor and the tetrahedron argument that produces it; pressure as the isotropic part; the symmetry of the stress tensor as angular-momentum balance. Strain, and Hooke's law reduced by isotropy to two constants. Mass and momentum conservation in local form. Euler's equations for an inviscid fluid, with Navier-Stokes stated and the viscous term identified. Sound as the linearisation of Euler's equations about rest. P- and S-waves in an elastic solid, and why only solids carry shear waves — which is how the Earth's liquid outer core was found.
units.math_tools: The divergence theorem as the engine that converts every integral conservation statement into a local one: continuity, and momentum balance with the stress tensor supplying the flux. The material derivative and the transport theorem. Tensor fields on R^3, the first use of unit 16's index machinery on a field rather than a single object. Cauchy's stress theorem proved by the tetrahedron limit — the only place in classical physics where you *prove* rather than assume that a physical quantity is bilinear, and the best rehearsal available for what T^{mu nu} is. Flagged explicitly: the triple (energy density, momentum density, momentum flux) assembled here becomes T^{mu nu} in unit 35, and this local conservation law is exactly the statement that its divergence vanishes.
units.worked_example: Derive the speed of sound: linearise continuity and Euler about rest, close the system with the adiabatic relation p proportional to rho^gamma, and obtain c = sqrt(gamma p/rho) = 343 m/s in air at 20 C. Then show Newton's isothermal assumption yields 280 m/s, 18 per cent low — a discrepancy that stood unexplained for a century until Laplace, and a genuine historical falsification with a number attached and a wrong physical hypothesis identifiable as its cause.
units.problem_set: Constructing local conservation laws and linearising. "Cauchy's tetrahedron": prove the traction on a surface is linear in its normal, hence a tensor, then prove that tensor symmetric from angular-momentum balance and identify the assumption (no intrinsic body torques) that derivation quietly uses. "Seismology": compute P- and S-wave speeds from given Lame parameters, show c_L > c_T always, and explain why the S-wave shadow zone implies a liquid core; locate an epicentre from P-S arrival differences at three stations.
units.checkpoint: From an integral conservation statement you derive its local form by the divergence theorem, you prove Cauchy's theorem rather than assuming stress is bilinear, and you compute the speed of sound in air to within 2 per cent — getting the thermodynamic closure right rather than lucky.

units.title: Static fields: electrostatics and magnetostatics, the same vector calculus twice
units.physics: Coulomb's law and its formal identity with Newton's, so that all of unit 05 transfers free of charge and the differences — two signs, and no shielding of gravity, so gravity accumulates while electricity screens — are the interesting part. Conductors and boundary conditions; the method of images; the multipole expansion of a charge distribution, reusing unit 10's Legendre machinery as a boundary-value tool. Magnetostatics: Biot-Savart, Ampere's law, the vector potential, gauge freedom, and the empirical fact that B has no sources, which has no electrostatic analogue. The Lorentz force, connecting back to unit 12's velocity-dependent potential.
units.math_tools: Stokes' theorem doing real work at last: Ampere's law is the curl theorem applied to B. Poisson's and Laplace's equations; Green's functions for the Laplacian in two and three dimensions, with the dimension-dependence derived rather than asserted; uniqueness by the maximum principle; Earnshaw's theorem. Separation of variables in spherical and cylindrical coordinates using unit 19's machinery. The existence of A from div B = 0 as the Poincare lemma, with the solenoid supplying the non-simply-connected obstruction — the same computation as unit 04's vortex, one degree up. The Helmholtz decomposition: a field decaying at infinity is determined by its divergence and its curl, which is why Maxwell's system has exactly four equations and is neither over- nor under-determined, a point almost never made explicitly.
units.worked_example: A grounded conducting sphere in a uniform external field: solve Laplace's equation by Legendre expansion, extract the induced dipole moment and the surface charge density proportional to cos(theta); then obtain the identical answer by images with two image charges, and reconcile the two derivations term by term.
units.problem_set: Boundary-value problems, the structure theorem, and the first cohomological hint. "Images and their limits": solve the point charge near a grounded plane and near a grounded sphere, then exhibit a geometry admitting no finite image set. "The solenoid": compute B inside and outside, find B = 0 outside but A nonzero with circulation equal to the enclosed flux, and identify this as unit 04's vortex problem with the field one degree higher — closed but not exact. "Helmholtz precisely": state the decomposition with its decay hypotheses, prove uniqueness, and use it to predict that Maxwell's system must have four equations before you have seen them.
units.checkpoint: You solve a spherical boundary-value problem by Legendre expansion and independently by images and get the same answer, produce a vector potential in a stated gauge, and state the Helmholtz theorem with its hypotheses and use it to count Maxwell's equations in advance.

units.title: Maxwell: the displacement current, and light
units.physics: Faraday's law and induction. Maxwell's repair: Ampere's law is inconsistent with charge conservation for time-dependent currents, and demanding consistency forces the displacement current — a term added on purely logical grounds whose consequence is the existence of light. The complete system. Field energy and momentum; Poynting's theorem as local energy conservation; the Maxwell stress tensor, which is the first energy-momentum tensor in the course. Plane waves and polarisation. Potentials and gauge freedom; Lorenz and Coulomb gauges; retarded potentials; the Larmor formula and dipole radiation.
units.math_tools: The wave operator and its retarded Green's function in three dimensions, computed by unit 20's contour methods rather than asserted — the i-epsilon prescription is the place where causality enters the mathematics and it is made explicit. Kirchhoff's formula and the method of descent; the strong Huygens principle, so that sharp wavefronts exist in three dimensions and not in two. Gauge transformations as redundancy of description, with the gauge-invariant fields carrying the physical content and the residual freedom in Lorenz gauge made explicit.
units.worked_example: Derive the displacement current: take the divergence of Ampere's law as Ampere left it, find it contradicts charge conservation, and show exactly one term repairs it. Then derive the vacuum wave equation and compute c = 1/sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0) = 2.998e8 m/s from two bench-top constants, comparing with Fizeau's 1849 measurement of 3.13e8 — the moment light became an electromagnetic phenomenon — and estimate how good the measurements had to be for the identification to convince anyone in 1862.
units.problem_set: Field computations, gauge, energy accounting and radiation. "Same fields, two gauges": compute the potentials of a point charge in Lorenz and in Coulomb gauge, note the Coulomb-gauge scalar potential is instantaneous, and show E and B are nevertheless identical and causal. "Huygens fails in two dimensions": obtain the 2D wave Green's function by descent from 3D and show it is supported inside the light cone, not on it, so a two-dimensional flash has a fading tail. "Larmor": derive the radiated power of an accelerated charge and show a classical orbiting electron collapses in 1.6e-11 s — a failure this course records and deliberately does not repair.
units.checkpoint: You derive the displacement current from charge conservation alone, obtain the vacuum wave equation and c from epsilon_0 and mu_0, compute the retarded Green's function by contour integration with a defensible account of why that prescription is the causal one, and show two different gauges produce identical E and B.

units.title: The crisis: Maxwell's equations do not survive a Galilean boost
units.physics: Galilean relativity, which unit 03 assumed without naming. The problem: Maxwell's equations contain c with no frame attached, and they change form under x -> x - vt. Three responses and their fates — an ether, with its absurd required properties; emission theories, killed by de Sitter's binary stars; and modifying Maxwell, killed by Maxwell continuing to be right. Michelson-Morley's null result; Kennedy-Thorndike and Ives-Stilwell and what each independently pins down. Stellar aberration and Fizeau's moving water, which no ether model ever explained together. Lorentz's contraction hypothesis and local time as a patch, and Poincare's realisation that the patches form a group.
units.math_tools: What covariance of a PDE system under a group action means precisely. Direct computation: apply the chain rule for a Galilean boost to the wave operator and exhibit the cross terms that appear; then ask which linear substitution kills them, and derive the Lorentz transformation as the answer — before any postulate has been stated. Symmetry groups of differential operators, with the conformal group of the wave equation mentioned as the larger answer.
units.worked_example: Transform the one-dimensional wave equation under a Galilean boost, display the extra terms, and show no choice of v removes them. Then solve for the general linear map on (x,t) preserving the operator's form: two conditions, a one-parameter family, and the Lorentz transformation emerges with c fixed by the equation itself — Einstein's postulate arriving as a conclusion rather than an assumption. This is the unit that lets unit 26 say 'the invariant speed is c' rather than 'assume the invariant speed is c'.
units.problem_set: Invariance computations and the experimental record. "Michelson-Morley quantitatively": compute the expected fringe shift for the 1887 apparatus under a 30 km/s ether wind (about 0.4 fringes), compare with the measured bound below 0.01, and state what Lorentz contraction alone would have predicted. "Which experiment pins which": show Michelson-Morley alone is consistent with several transformation laws, and identify exactly what Kennedy-Thorndike and Ives-Stilwell each add.
units.checkpoint: You show by direct computation that the wave equation is not Galilean-invariant and is Lorentz-invariant, and derive the boost by demanding form-invariance — without assuming the constancy of c as a postulate.

units.title: Minkowski space: relativity as the geometry of a quadratic form
units.physics: Einstein's two postulates and the work each does. The relativity of simultaneity as the actual content, with time dilation and length contraction as corollaries rather than postulates. The invariant interval. The twin paradox. The pole and the barn. Velocity addition, relativistic Doppler, aberration and the headlight effect. Causal structure: which parts of 'before' survive and which do not, so that no superluminal signalling is a theorem. A note on provenance: unit 25 *earned* the invariant speed's value from Maxwell; a learner who has not done unit 25 takes it on credit here, and the course says so rather than pretending otherwise.
units.math_tools: Derive the Lorentz group from structural assumptions alone: homogeneity gives linearity, isotropy and the group axioms give a one-parameter family with a single invariant speed as the only free parameter, and unit 25's wave operator fixes it at c. Then the bilinear form eta of signature (-,+,+,+); O(1,3) and its four connected components; the proper orthochronous subgroup; boosts as hyperbolic rotations with rapidity as the additive parameter, so velocity addition is nothing but the addition formula for tanh. The Alexandrov-Zeeman theorem cited: preserving causal order alone already forces the Lorentz group up to scale. Minkowski diagrams with correctly scaled axes and calibration hyperbolae, which is the only way the diagrams do not lie. The reversed triangle inequality for timelike curves, proved.
units.worked_example: The twin paradox three ways, all agreeing: by evaluating proper time tau = integral sqrt(-eta_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu) along each worldline; by counting Doppler-shifted signals each twin receives, which makes the asymmetry visible as the moment the shift flips and needs no appeal to acceleration at all; and on a Minkowski diagram, tracking the travelling twin's lines of simultaneity as they jump across the turnaround. Then the general point: because the signature is Lorentzian, timelike geodesics locally *maximise* proper time — the opposite of the Riemannian case, and the sign that makes unit 32's geodesic principle a maximum principle. Worth being uncomfortable about for ten minutes.
units.problem_set: Boosts, rapidity, and causal structure taken seriously. "Rapidity is additive": prove velocity addition is tanh addition and compute the speed after ten successive 0.5c boosts. "The barn": resolve the pole-and-barn paradox by writing both door closings as events and transforming them, showing the disagreement concerns simultaneity and no contradiction exists. "No superluminal signalling": show that spacelike-separated events have their order reversed in some frame, hence a faster-than-light signal is a backwards-in-time signal in another frame, and show the argument fails for timelike separation.
units.checkpoint: You derive the Lorentz transformation from homogeneity, isotropy, the group axioms and one invariant speed, compute proper time along any specified worldline, and prove the twin paradox is the reversed triangle inequality for timelike curves in eta.

units.title: Relativistic dynamics: four-vectors, and why colliders exist
units.physics: Four-velocity, four-acceleration, four-momentum. E = gamma m c^2, rest energy, and the case against 'relativistic mass'. Invariant mass as the norm of a system's total four-momentum, which is why a box of hot gas weighs more.
