Conservation of four-momentum in collisions; thresholds; Compton scattering; decay; the relativistic rocket. Massless particles and why they must travel at c. Why a rigid body is impossible in relativity — Born rigidity and the Ehrenfest disc — and hence why unit 16 has no relativistic successor. Hyperbolic motion at constant proper acceleration and its Rindler horizon, which costs nothing here and is unit 30's main tool.
units.math_tools: Four-vectors as elements of a vector space carrying a representation of the Lorentz group, with the invariant pairing giving minus m^2 c^2. Proper time as arc length in Lorentzian signature; the constraint u dot u = -c^2 and its consequence that acceleration is always orthogonal to velocity. The free-particle action S = -mc times the integral of d(tau), and its Euler-Lagrange equations by unit 11 yielding p = gamma m v — the first Lagrangian in the course that is not T - V and does not come from a metric on configuration space, which is the point of departure. Legendre-transforming it by unit 14 to H = sqrt(p^2c^2 + m^2c^4), noting how nearly degenerate the massless case is. Mandelstam invariants and the systematic technique of squaring conservation equations to work frame-free.
units.worked_example: The antiproton threshold: p + p -> p + p + p + antiproton requires s at least (4 m_p c^2)^2. Evaluate s in the fixed-target frame to get a beam kinetic energy of about 5.6 GeV, and in the collider frame to get 2 x 0.94 GeV — the factor-of-three argument that justified building colliders, and the reason the Bevatron was designed at 6.2 GeV. Three lines, no frame transformation at all.
units.problem_set: Invariant technique, thresholds, and one instructive wrong answer. "Compton": derive the wavelength shift from four-momentum conservation and the photon's null four-momentum in four lines. "Mass is not additive": for two photons of energy E travelling oppositely compute the pair's invariant mass 2E/c^2 and explain what happens as the angle closes. "Relativistic Kepler precesses": solve the orbit for a 1/r potential with relativistic kinematics, obtain a perihelion advance, and note it is roughly one sixth of Mercury's observed residual — the single most instructive wrong answer in physics, because it shows time dilation alone is not gravity. Unit 37 supplies the other five sixths.
units.checkpoint: You compute a reaction threshold by evaluating the invariant s in whichever frame is easiest and compare it with a published accelerator design energy, and derive p = gamma m v from the action -mc times proper time by the Euler-Lagrange equations of unit 11.

units.title: Electromagnetism was relativistic all along: the field tensor
units.physics: E and B are not two fields but one field seen from a frame. The field tensor F^{mu nu} and the transformation rules; a purely magnetic field in one frame is partly electric in another. Purcell's argument: the magnetic force between a current and a moving charge is electrostatics plus length contraction, so magnetism is what relativity does to Coulomb's law at v/c around 1e-13, amplified by the number of charges in a wire. The covariant Maxwell equations, four collapsing to two. The Lorentz force as dp^mu/d(tau) = q F u. The field's stress-energy tensor, its symmetry, tracelessness, and vanishing divergence — the same statement as unit 22's continuum balance, now with energy included. Radiation reaction named, and the Abraham-Lorentz runaway solutions flagged honestly as unresolved in classical theory.
units.math_tools: Tensor fields on Minkowski space; raising and lowering with eta, the first place where unit 16's distinction between vectors and covectors is not optional. The antisymmetric (0,2)-tensor and its six components. The Levi-Civita symbol versus the Levi-Civita tensor; the dual tensor; the two invariants, one proportional to B^2 - E^2/c^2 and the other to E dot B. The four-current and continuity as a vanishing divergence. This is where abstract index notation becomes fluent, and that fluency is the actual prerequisite for units 32 through 37.
units.worked_example: The wire and the test charge, in full: in the lab frame a neutral current-carrying wire exerts a magnetic force on a charge moving parallel to it; boost to the charge's rest frame, where the positive and negative line densities contract differently, the wire acquires a net charge, and the force is purely electrostatic. Show the two forces agree down to the last factor of gamma in the transverse-force transformation. Then verify that the vanishing divergence of T^{mu nu} reproduces exactly Poynting's theorem for the time component and the Maxwell stress balance for the spatial ones.
units.problem_set: Index gymnastics and field transformations. "Which field can you transform away?": given E and B in one frame, use the two invariants to decide whether a frame exists in which the field is purely electric, purely magnetic, or neither, and construct the boost when it exists. "Larmor, covariantly": derive the Lienard generalisation of Larmor's formula from the invariant a dot a and check it reduces correctly in the non-relativistic limit.
units.checkpoint: Given the field tensor and a boost you derive the E and B transformation rules and verify both invariants numerically, and you show by explicit computation that the divergence of the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor vanishes and reproduces the familiar conservation laws.

units.title: Classical field theory: Noether again, and where T^{mu nu} actually comes from
units.physics: A field is a mechanical system whose coordinates are labelled by points of space rather than by an index. The action as an integral of a Lagrangian density over spacetime. Three Lagrangians done explicitly: the scalar wave equation, the Klein-Gordon field, and Maxwell's L = -(1/4 mu_0) F_{mu nu}F^{mu nu} - A_mu J^mu, from which the source equations follow in four lines. Gauge invariance as a property of the action, forcing current conservation. Noether for fields: continuous symmetries give conserved currents and hence charges. Spacetime translation gives the canonical energy-momentum tensor — which for Maxwell comes out neither symmetric nor gauge-invariant, a genuinely surprising defect — and the Belinfante-Rosenfeld improvement repairs it. Then the definition general relativity actually uses: T^{mu nu} = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta S_matter/delta g_{mu nu}, automatically symmetric and gauge-invariant. This unit exists so that the right-hand side of Einstein's equation is a definition rather than an incantation.
units.math_tools: Functional derivatives of an action over a spacetime region; the field Euler-Lagrange equations derived by unit 11's argument in four dimensions with the boundary term handled explicitly. Noether's theorem in the field-theoretic setting, proved in full. Variation with respect to a metric, introduced here in flat space with g held general, so that unit 35's Einstein-Hilbert variation is a continuation rather than a new technique. Tensor densities, sqrt(-g) and the invariant volume element.
units.worked_example: Derive all of Maxwell's source equations by varying S with respect to A_mu, carefully, including the integration by parts and the boundary term. Then compute T^{mu nu} twice: once as the canonical Noether current from translation invariance, obtaining the non-symmetric non-gauge-invariant expression; once by metric variation, obtaining the familiar symmetric F^{mu alpha}F^nu_alpha - (1/4) eta^{mu nu} F^2 — and identify the Belinfante improvement term as exactly the difference. The two routes landing in the same place by different mathematics is the point.
units.problem_set: Building actions and extracting currents. "The Klein-Gordon field": from L = -(1/2)(d phi)^2 - (1/2) m^2 phi^2 derive the field equation, the energy-momentum tensor and the dispersion relation, and interpret the mass term as what makes the wave equation dispersive. "A symmetry with no obvious charge": find the conserved current of the global phase symmetry of a complex scalar, then show that gauging it — letting the phase depend on x — forces the introduction of a field with exactly the transformation law of A_mu.
units.checkpoint: Given a Lagrangian density you derive the field equations, construct the Noether current of every continuous symmetry and verify its conservation on shell, and produce the symmetric energy-momentum tensor by metric variation — and for Maxwell you can state precisely how the canonical and metric-variation tensors differ and why the difference is separately conserved.

units.title: The equivalence principle, and why flat spacetime cannot hold gravity
units.physics: Inertial and gravitational mass coincide to one part in 1e15, from Eotvos through Adelberger's torsion balances to MICROSCOPE. Einstein's elevator; the weak, Einstein and strong forms stated separately because they are genuinely different claims, with an experiment that distinguishes them. Consequences derived before any geometry exists: light bends, clocks low down run slow, light climbing loses frequency. Pound-Rebka. GPS as a working system that fails without both corrections. Then the argument that ends the part: tidal forces cannot be transformed away, so there is no global inertial frame, so gravity is not a force field on Minkowski space.
units.math_tools: Accelerated observers in Minkowski space; proper acceleration; the hyperbolic worldline from unit 27. Rindler coordinates and the metric with a position-dependent lapse — a non-constant metric on a *flat* spacetime, which is precisely the point that non-constant metric components are not yet gravity, and the standard inoculation against the beginner's belief that coordinate effects are physics. The Rindler horizon. Ehrenfest's rotating disc, whose spatial geometry already has circumference over diameter greater than pi, so a rotating frame in flat spacetime already forces non-Euclidean spatial geometry. Unit 05's tidal tensor restated as the object no coordinate change removes — the first curvature invariant, met before curvature is defined.
units.worked_example: Derive the gravitational redshift from the equivalence principle alone: in a uniformly accelerating rocket a signal takes h/c to reach the ceiling, by which time the ceiling has gained speed gh/c, so the fractional shift is gh/c^2. Evaluate for Harvard's 22.5 m tower: 2.46e-15, against Pound and Rebka's measured (2.57 +/- 0.26)e-15. Then the GPS budget: +45.7 microseconds per day gravitational, -7.2 kinematic, net +38.5 — about 11 km of position error per day if ignored.
units.problem_set: Equivalence-principle derivations and the Rindler wedge. "Rindler": derive the coordinates from the hyperbolic worldline, find the horizon, and show a signal from beyond it never arrives — a horizon with no gravity anywhere in sight. "Tides are the real thing": show a transformation to a freely falling frame kills the first derivatives of the metric but cannot kill the second, and identify the surviving object, thereby proving that 'gravity is not a force' and 'gravity is real' are both true. "Why not a tensor field on flat space": show a spin-2 field on Minkowski coupled to stress-energy must couple to its own stress-energy, and state what that self-consistency demands (Deser's argument, whose iteration produces general relativity).
units.checkpoint: You derive the gravitational redshift from the equivalence principle with no geometry and match Pound-Rebka within its error bar, state the three equivalence principles with an experiment distinguishing them, and exhibit a non-constant metric on flat spacetime — thereby proving that non-constant metric components alone are not gravity.

units.title: Manifolds: doing all of it without coordinates
units.physics: Configuration space from unit 12 was a manifold all along — the double pendulum's is a torus and the rigid body's is SO(3) x R^3, which is why Euler angles have coordinate singularities rather than because anyone was careless. Spacetime as a manifold with no preferred coordinates, and an honest account of why general covariance, on its own, says considerably less than it sounds like.
units.math_tools: Smooth manifolds, charts, atlases, smooth maps, diffeomorphisms. Tangent vectors defined three ways — equivalence classes of curves, derivations of germs, coordinate n-tuples with a transformation law — with the isomorphisms constructed, because reconciling them is what makes the physics literature readable. The differential of a smooth map; the cotangent space; one-forms and the dual basis; df as the canonical example. Tensor fields as sections, with unit 16's transformation law recovered as nothing more than a change of basis, so that 'transforms like a tensor' becomes a theorem rather than a definition. Vector fields as derivations and as flows; the Lie bracket and its interpretation as the failure of flows to commute; the Lie derivative of tensors by pullback along the flow. Killing vector fields defined as those with L_X g = 0, planted here for unit 36. Submanifolds, embeddings, the Frobenius theorem. Cited, not proved: partitions of unity, Whitney, the hairy ball theorem.
units.worked_example: The two-sphere with two stereographic charts: write one vector field in each, verify the components transform by the Jacobian on the overlap, and show no single chart covers the sphere. Write the round metric in both charts and check they agree. Compute the flow of the rotation field d/d(phi) and verify L_{d/d phi} g = 0 by direct computation, so it is a Killing field — the first instance of the object that will make Schwarzschild's conserved energy and angular momentum appear in unit 36. Then compute the Lie bracket of two rotation generators and recover so(3) from unit 16, now realised by flows rather than matrices.
units.problem_set: Charts, transformations and brackets. "Components are not the tensor": give nine functions on the sphere in one chart, transform them, and decide whether they define a tensor field. "Lie derivative versus partial derivative": show by explicit computation that L_X T is a tensor while d_mu T^{nu rho} is not, and identify which terms in the Lie derivative are exactly the ones repairing the transformation law. "The torus is a configuration space": write the double pendulum's configuration space as T^2, produce an atlas, and express its kinetic energy as a metric in each chart.
units.checkpoint: You construct an atlas for a given manifold and verify the transition maps smooth, define a tensor field in one chart and transform it to another verifying agreement on the overlap, compute Lie brackets and Lie derivatives in coordinates, and determine whether a given vector field is Killing for a given metric.

units.title: Metric, connection, geodesics — free fall is a straight line
units.physics: Free fall is geodesic motion; the geodesic equation replaces Newton's second law. Parallel transport is what an ideal gyroscope does. The Christoffel symbols as the 'gravitational field' that can be made to vanish at a point but not in a neighbourhood — which is the equivalence principle stated as a fact about connections. The Newtonian limit, recovering d^2x/dt^2 = -grad Phi with g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi/c^2) and the factor of two everyone gets wrong once. Minimal coupling and the comma-goes-to-semicolon rule, with the ordering ambiguity flagged honestly, and the pleasant observation that dF = 0 needs no modification because the exterior derivative never needed a connection. The structural point that geodesic motion is not an independent postulate: a vanishing divergence of T for a localised source already implies its worldline is a geodesic.
units.math_tools: The metric tensor and the geometry it defines: lengths, angles, volume form, raising and lowering. The problem that the partial derivative of a vector field is not tensorial. Affine connections and the covariant derivative on tensors of every type, with sign conventions fixed once; torsion; metric compatibility. The fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry proved via the Koszul formula, so the Christoffel symbols are derived rather than posited — six lines, and the single formula the rest of the course computes with. Parallel transport along a curve as an ODE. Geodesics two ways — auto-parallel and stationary points of length or energy by unit 11 — with the equivalence proved and the affine-parameter subtlety handled rather than waved past. Normal coordinates and the local flatness theorem: at any point one can set g to eta with vanishing first derivatives but not vanishing second derivatives, which is exactly why curvature survives, and exactly the mathematical content of the equivalence principle.
units.worked_example: Geodesics of the round sphere are great circles, derived twice — by the auto-parallel equation with computed Christoffel symbols, and by extremising arc length — and shown to agree. Then the practical trick used for the rest of the course: write the geodesic Lagrangian, take its Euler-Lagrange equations, and read the Christoffel symbols straight off, demonstrated on the Schwarzschild form before that solution has been derived. Then recover Newton: take g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi/c^2), g_ij = delta_ij, expand the geodesic equation to lowest order in v/c and in Phi/c^2, and watch Newton's law appear with the factor of two fixed by requiring exactly that.
units.problem_set: Connection computations and parallel transport. "Christoffels by Lagrangian": compute every Christoffel symbol of a given metric by the geodesic-Lagrangian trick, check against the coordinate formula, and count the arithmetic saved. "Transport around a loop": parallel-transport a vector around a spherical triangle and find the holonomy angle equals the enclosed area — unit 33 arriving a week early. "Flat in disguise": compute the connection for ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d(theta)^2 and confirm it is polar coordinates on a plane rather than curvature.
units.checkpoint: For a given metric you compute every Christoffel symbol by the geodesic-Lagrangian trick and verify against the coordinate formula, prove the Levi-Civita connection is the unique torsion-free metric-compatible one, construct normal coordinates at a point and state exactly what can and cannot be made to vanish there, and recover Newton's law from the geodesic equation with the correct factor in g_00.

units.title: Curvature: tidal forces, with the mask off
units.physics: Geodesic deviation: two nearby freely falling particles accelerate relative to one another at a rate given by the Riemann tensor. Set this beside unit 05's Newtonian tidal equation and read off the identification of R^i_{0j0} with the second derivatives of the Newtonian potential — the single most important correspondence in the course, and the reason curvature is not an analogy for gravity but the same computation. Curvature as the thing no coordinate change removes, and therefore as the honest definition of a gravitational field. Why in three dimensions Ricci determines Riemann completely, and hence why there are no vacuum gravitational waves in 3D.
units.math_tools: The Riemann tensor defined by the commutator of covariant derivatives, with the check that it is tensorial despite being built from derivatives. Its symmetries and the component count n^2(n^2-1)/12 — 20 in four dimensions, 6 in three, 1 in two. The first and second Bianchi identities. Sectional and Gaussian curvature; Gauss's Theorema Egregium as the statement that curvature is intrinsic. The Ricci tensor, the scalar curvature, and the Weyl tensor as the trace-free part carrying vacuum tidal effects. The Einstein tensor, and the fact that its divergence vanishes identically as a consequence of the contracted second Bianchi identity rather than by assumption — highlighted, because it is what selects Einstein's equation in unit 35.
units.worked_example: Compute the Riemann tensor of the two-sphere of radius a from its metric, confirm the single independent component gives Gaussian curvature 1/a^2, and verify that unit 32's spherical-triangle holonomy equals the integral of curvature over it. Then derive geodesic deviation from scratch, apply it to two great circles leaving the equator a small distance apart to get xi'' = -xi/a^2 (they converge and cross at the pole — that *is* tidal force), and show that in the weak-field limit it reproduces unit 05's tidal eigenvalues (-2, 1, 1)GM/r^3 term for term.
units.problem_set: Curvature computations and the Newtonian correspondence. "One component in two dimensions": prove a 2-surface's Riemann tensor has exactly one independent component and compute it for the hyperbolic plane. "Counting components": prove the count n^2(n^2-1)/12 from the symmetries alone, evaluate at n = 2, 3, 4, and explain why Ricci determines Riemann in three dimensions. "Bianchi does the work": prove the Einstein tensor divergence-free from the contracted second Bianchi identity, and note this is the only reason unit 35's field equations can be consistent at all.
units.checkpoint: You compute the Riemann tensor of a 2-surface and verify it has exactly one independent component, prove the contracted Bianchi identity, and show the geodesic deviation equation reduces to unit 05's Newtonian tidal equation with the correct identification of components.

units.title: Differential forms and Cartan: Stokes' theorem was always one theorem
units.physics: Maxwell as dF = 0 and d(star F) proportional to the current — four equations becoming two, with the first an identity once F = dA, and gauge freedom becoming exactness. Charge conservation as the same identity applied to the other pair. Magnetic monopoles as a cohomological obstruction to writing F = dA globally. Unit 14's symplectic form as an actual object, with Liouville's theorem as the closedness of its top power, proved in one line by Cartan's magic formula next to the divergence proof. Unit 23's solenoid as a de Rham class.
units.math_tools: The exterior algebra; k-forms; the wedge product; the exterior derivative characterised axiomatically with d^2 = 0 from Clairaut; pullbacks and the naturality of d, which is why forms are worth the trouble. Orientation, volume forms, integration over manifolds. The generalised Stokes theorem, stated once and proved on the cube, with the gradient theorem of unit 04, Green's theorem, the curl theorem of unit 23 and the divergence theorem of unit 05 recovered as its low-dimensional cases and the full dictionary to grad, div and curl written out. Closed and exact; the Poincare lemma; de Rham cohomology, with H^1 of the punctured plane computed — closing the question unit 04 deliberately left open. The Hodge star and the metric's role in it, with the sign worked out in signature (-,+,+,+). Cartan's structure equations as a faster route to curvature, with one worked comparison against unit 33's coordinate computation.
units.worked_example: Rewrite all four of Maxwell's equations in form language and expand them back into components, recovering the originals exactly including every factor and sign. Then compute the de Rham class of unit 04's vortex field, show it is closed but not exact, and identify its circulation 2 pi as the pairing of its class with the generator of first homology — the question asked thirty units earlier, answered.
units.problem_set: Form manipulation, cohomology, and a speed comparison. "d squared in disguise": show the homogeneous Maxwell pair is the identity ddA = 0, and that charge conservation is the same identity applied to the other pair. "Compute a cohomology": find H^1 of the punctured plane and of the torus, and say which physical statement each dimension encodes. "Cartan versus Christoffel": recompute the curvature of one metric from unit 33 by moving frames and structure equations, and count the arithmetic saved.
units.checkpoint: You express Maxwell's four equations as dF = 0 and d(star F) = mu_0 star J, expand them back into components recovering the originals exactly, compute H^1 of the punctured plane — closing unit 04's open question — and reproduce one of unit 33's curvature computations by Cartan's structure equations.

units.title: The Einstein field equations, twice
units.physics: The requirements listed before any equation is written: a tensor equation so no coordinates are preferred; second order in the metric so the initial-value problem is the familiar kind; sourced by everything carrying energy and momentum, because E = mc^2; automatically compatible with local conservation since the divergence of T vanishes; and reducing to Poisson's equation in the weak, slow, static limit. The stress-energy tensor made concrete for dust, a perfect fluid and — for those who have done unit 29 — the electromagnetic field, with unit 22's continuum momentum balance recognisable as its non-relativistic shadow. The equations with the cosmological term, whose history and current status as dark energy are stated without editorialising. The vacuum equations R_{mu nu} = 0, and the crucial observation that they are not trivial because the Weyl tensor survives. Coordinate freedom and the count 10 - 4 - 4 = 2. Why global energy conservation genuinely fails in general spacetimes rather than merely looking difficult. Choquet-Bruhat's well-posed initial-value formulation cited, since it is not obvious and took forty years.
units.math_tools: Route one, requiring unit 29: the Einstein-Hilbert action varied with respect to the inverse metric — the identity for the variation of the metric determinant, the Palatini identity, the total-derivative term that becomes the Gibbons-Hawking-York boundary contribution, and T defined as the variational derivative of the matter action, which is unit 29's definition, so the two units lock together. Route two, requiring only units 33 and 30: the contracted Bianchi identity hands you a divergence-free second-order symmetric tensor, and Lovelock's theorem says that in four dimensions the Einstein tensor plus a cosmological term is the only one — so the equation is forced rather than chosen, and the coupling is fixed by the Newtonian limit. A learner arriving without unit 29 gets route two, which is complete but does not explain where the right-hand side comes from; the unit says so plainly.
units.worked_example: The Newtonian limit in complete detail: perturb the metric about eta, take the field static and the test particles slow, use unit 32's geodesic result g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi/c^2), compute the relevant Ricci component to first order, and show the field equation becomes Poisson's equation — which is the only thing that fixes the coupling at 8 pi G/c^4. Then, for those on route one, vary the Einstein-Hilbert action from beginning to end with nothing skipped and watch the same constant appear. Two different routes to 8 pi G/c^4 is the kind of consistency check that makes a theory believable.
units.problem_set: Variation, uniqueness, and limits. "Which tensors are allowed": show Einstein's first guess, Ricci proportional to T, forces T to be trace-free by the Bianchi identity and is therefore wrong, then find the fix — reconstructing 1915 in one problem. "Vary it" (needs 29): derive the field equations from the Einstein-Hilbert action keeping every boundary term visible, and identify exactly where the Gibbons-Hawking-York term is needed and why. "Two polarisations, counted twice": obtain the plus and cross polarisations from the linearised vacuum equation in transverse-traceless gauge, then count independently as 10 minus 4 gauge minus 4 constraints and confirm the answers agree.
units.checkpoint: You argue from the contracted Bianchi identity and Lovelock's theorem why the Einstein tensor is forced, fix the coupling constant at 8 pi G/c^4 from the Newtonian limit, and linearise the equations to obtain the wave equation with the correct count of propagating degrees of freedom — and, if you have unit 29, you obtain the same field equations independently by varying the Einstein-Hilbert action.

units.title: Schwarzschild: the first exact solution, and what its two singularities are
units.physics: Static, spherically symmetric, vacuum. The Schwarzschild metric, derived rather than quoted. Birkhoff's theorem: spherical symmetry forces staticity, so a pulsating star radiates nothing and the interior of a spherical shell is exactly flat — the relativistic shell theorem, and the reason there is no monopole gravitational radiation. The Schwarzschild radius: 2.95 km for the Sun, 8.9 mm for the Earth. Proper versus coordinate radial distance and time, and what an infalling and a distant observer each report. The event horizon as a one-way null surface with nothing locally remarkable about it, and the finite proper time to the singularity.
units.math_tools: Solving the vacuum equations with the ansatz ds^2 = -A(r)dt^2 + B(r)dr^2 + r^2 d(Omega)^2 — the full computation, done once, slowly, with every nonzero Christoffel and Ricci component displayed, and the integration constant fixed by unit 35's Newtonian limit. Killing vectors as infinitesimal isometries, and the conserved quantities they produce along geodesics, giving E and L for free — which is unit 13's Noether theorem in geometric clothing, and worth saying out loud. Diagnosing singularities with invariants: the Kretschmann scalar 48G^2M^2/c^4r^6 is finite at the horizon and divergent only at the centre. Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates removing the horizon singularity; the Kruskal-Szekeres maximal extension and its four regions; conformal compactification and Penrose diagrams, constructed for Minkowski first so the technique is clear.
units.worked_example: Derive the Schwarzschild solution in full from the ansatz. Then show the horizon is a coordinate artefact by transforming explicitly to ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, while the centre survives every transformation because the Kretschmann scalar diverges as 1/r^6. Then build the Kruskal extension step by step — tortoise coordinate, null coordinates, exponential Kruskal coordinates — and draw the resulting diagram with all four regions.
units.problem_set: Geodesics, horizons and coordinates. "How long to fall": compute the proper time for radial infall from rest to the centre and show it is finite while the Schwarzschild coordinate time to reach the horizon diverges, then reconcile the two accounts without hand-waving. "Birkhoff": prove spherical symmetry plus vacuum forces staticity, and state the two consequences — no monopole radiation, and a flat shell interior. "Tidal death": compute the tidal tensor at the horizon as a function of M and find the mass above which a human survives horizon crossing.
units.checkpoint: You derive Schwarzschild from the ansatz, obtain the geodesic constants of motion from its Killing vectors and name the unit-13 theorem they are an instance of, and demonstrate by an explicit coordinate transformation plus an invariant scalar that exactly one of its two apparent singularities is real.

units.title: The classical tests: three numbers, and one of them is 43
units.physics: Geodesics in Schwarzschild. The effective potential with its new inverse-cube term and everything that follows: no stable circular orbit below six gravitational radii, a plunge with no Newtonian analogue, and precession of everything else. Mercury: 5600 arcsec per century observed, 5025 from the precession of the equinoxes, about 531 from the other planets by unit 10's perturbation machinery, and 43 left over that Le Verrier attributed to a planet nobody found. Light deflection: 1.75 arcsec at the solar limb, Eddington in 1919, and modern VLBI at 1.7510 +/- 0.0008. The Shapiro delay, measured by Cassini to one part in 1e5. Gravitational redshift, already settled in unit 30. The photon sphere at 3GM/c^2, which is the ring in the Event Horizon Telescope images. Modern tests named and dated: Gravity Probe B, GW150914, the S2 orbit around Sagittarius A*.
units.math_tools: Null and timelike geodesic equations from unit 36's Killing conserved quantities. The orbit equation u'' + u = GM/L^2 + 3GM u^2/c^2 — exactly unit 08's Binet equation with one extra term, which is the cleanest possible statement of what general relativity adds to Newton. Unit 21's Poincare-Lindstedt method in its intended use: the secular term is the whole answer, giving 6 pi GM/c^2 a(1-e^2) per orbit. The null case with an impact parameter giving 4GM/c^2 b, and the explicit comparison with the Newtonian-corpuscle calculation, which gives exactly half — so the factor of two is the discriminating prediction, and it comes from the spatial part of the metric.
units.worked_example: Mercury end to end, with a number: from the metric to the orbit equation to the perturbative solution to the answer, using a = 5.79e10 m, e = 0.2056 and 415.2 orbits per century, arriving at 42.98 arcsec per century against the observed 42.98 +/- 0.04. Then light deflection both ways — 0.87 arcsec as a Newtonian corpuscle, 1.75 in general relativity — identifying precisely which metric component supplies the missing half.
units.problem_set: Geodesic computations and tests against real data with real uncertainties. "The ISCO": find the innermost stable circular orbit at six gravitational radii from the effective potential and compute the binding energy there, 5.7 per cent of rest mass, which is the efficiency of a thin accretion disc, and compare with the observed radiative efficiency of accreting black holes. "Shapiro from Cassini": compute the round-trip radar delay for a signal grazing the Sun, evaluate for the 2002 superior conjunction geometry, and compare with the published measurement including its stated uncertainty.
units.checkpoint: From scratch, with no formula looked up, you compute Mercury's perihelion advance to within 1 arcsec per century of 43 and the solar light deflection as 1.75 arcsec, show the latter is exactly twice the Newtonian value and name the metric component responsible — and you can say why unit 21 forbade you from removing the secular term.

units.title: Gravitational waves
units.physics: Linearised general relativity. Gauge freedom as infinitesimal diffeomorphism — structurally the same redundancy as unit 24's electromagnetic gauge, and worth meeting twice for exactly that reason. Transverse-traceless gauge; two polarisations; the effect on a ring of free test masses. The quadrupole formula, and the structural reason there is no dipole radiation where electromagnetism has one: mass conservation kills the monopole and momentum conservation kills the dipole, so gravity's lowest radiating multipole is two orders up, which is why the waves are so weak. The Hulse-Taylor binary's orbital decay matching prediction to 0.2 per cent over forty years. LIGO's GW150914: strain 1e-21, three solar masses radiated in 0.2 s. The detector is a Michelson interferometer, so the same experiment that found no ether found gravitational waves.
units.math_tools: Perturbation to first order; the trace-reversed perturbation and its sourced wave equation; the retarded solution using exactly the Green's function unit 24 computed by unit 20's contour methods. The transverse-traceless projector and an honest degree-of-freedom count: ten components, minus four gauge, minus four residual, equals two. Multipole expansion of the source in the slow-motion limit. Unit 21's two-timing for the adiabatic inspiral. Why the energy carried by a wave is not a local tensor, the Isaacson average, and what that says about the phrase 'energy of the gravitational field'.
units.worked_example: The inspiral chirp: compute the quadrupole moment of a circular binary, get P = 32 G^4 mu^2 M^3/5c^5 r^5, balance against the orbital energy to obtain dr/dt, integrate to the coalescence time, and derive f-dot proportional to f^{11/3} with the chirp mass as the only combination that appears. Evaluate for PSR B1913+16 and obtain an orbital period derivative of -2.40e-12 against the measured -2.423e-12.
units.problem_set: Linearisation, gauge counting and estimation. "Count to two": start from ten components and reduce to two by fixing the gauge twice, explicit about the residual freedom at each stage. "Why nobody built a laboratory source": compute the power radiated by a steel bar spun as fast as its tensile strength allows and compare with LIGO's sensitivity. "LIGO's number": estimate the strain from GW150914's parameters, compare with 1e-21, and compute how far a 4 km arm actually moves — about 1e-18 m.
units.checkpoint: You derive the linearised wave equation, reduce ten components to two by explicit gauge fixing, exhibit both polarisations' effect on a ring of test masses, and reproduce the Hulse-Taylor orbital decay rate to within 5 per cent of the measured value.

units.title: Cosmology
units.physics: The cosmological principle as an assumption, with the evidence for it (CMB isotropy to 1e-5, galaxy surveys) stated separately from the assumption itself, and the honest note that it concerns large scales only. FLRW geometry and the three spatial curvatures. The Friedmann equations read as an energy equation with an effective potential — a direct callback to unit 08, and the cheapest honest way to understand what a cosmological constant does. Matter, radiation and Lambda eras and their scalings. Cosmological redshift as the stretching of wavelengths, and why it is not a Doppler shift. The distance ladder, the Hubble parameter, and the current H_0 tension stated as an open observational problem. Big Bang nucleosynthesis as the earliest quantitative success. The horizon and flatness problems, with inflation presented with its motivation and its unresolved status.
units.math_tools: Maximally symmetric spaces and the uniqueness of the FLRW form. Computing the Einstein tensor for FLRW — substantial, entirely mechanical, and a good test of whether unit 33's machinery is fluent. Comoving and proper coordinates; conformal time. The fluid equation obtained both from the vanishing divergence of unit 22's perfect-fluid stress tensor and as a consequence of the two Friedmann equations. Solving for single-component and mixed universes; the age integral; particle and event horizons as integrals along the light cone.
units.worked_example: Derive both Friedmann equations from scratch — metric, Christoffels, Ricci, scalar curvature, then G = 8 pi G T with T = diag(-rho, p, p, p) — and read off the standard forms. Solve the three pure cases, then integrate the flat matter-plus-Lambda case with Planck's parameters (0.315, 0.685, H_0 = 67.4) to get 13.8 Gyr, and locate matter-Lambda equality at about z = 0.30, noting we live rather close to it.
units.problem_set: Cosmological computations against real numbers. "The age of the universe": integrate the Friedmann equation with the Planck parameters, then repeat with H_0 = 73 to see how much of the H_0 tension the age is sensitive to. "The horizon problem, quantified": compute the comoving particle horizon at recombination, convert it to an angle on today's sky, find roughly one degree, and state precisely why the observed uniformity across 180 degrees is therefore a problem.
units.checkpoint: You derive the Friedmann equations from FLRW plus Einstein without consulting a reference, solve for the scale factor in the matter-, radiation- and Lambda-dominated eras, and compute the age of the universe for the Planck parameters to within 0.3 Gyr of 13.8.

units.title: Rotating and charged holes, and where this course stops
units.physics: Kerr: frame dragging, the ergosphere, the two horizons, the Penrose process and its ceiling. Reissner-Nordstrom. No-hair, stated. Gravitational collapse (Oppenheimer-Snyder) and the Penrose diagram of a collapse-formed hole beside the eternal one, with the regions that are not physical identified. Trapped surfaces and the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems, stated with their energy conditions made explicit because that is precisely where they can fail. The four laws of black-hole mechanics and their thermodynamic reading; the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy and Hawking's temperature — stated as the point where this course's methods run out, since deriving them needs the quantum field theory the course has deliberately not taught.
units.math_tools: Killing horizons and surface gravity. The expansion of null congruences and Raychaudhuri's equation, stated and interpreted. Energy conditions (null, weak, strong, dominant) and which known matter violates which. The separability of Kerr geodesics by Hamilton-Jacobi and the resulting Carter constant — the payoff of branch unit 15, and the reason that branch exists at all.
units.worked_example: Locate the Kerr ergosphere, show no observer can remain static inside it, and compute the maximum energy extractable from an extremal hole by the Penrose process: 29.3 per cent of its mass. Then separate the Kerr Hamilton-Jacobi equation and exhibit the Carter constant as the fourth constant of motion that makes the system integrable in unit 17's precise sense.
units.problem_set: Horizon geometry and conserved quantities. "Carter's constant": separate the Kerr Hamilton-Jacobi equation, identify the fourth constant, and say what unit 17's Liouville-Arnold picture makes of a four-constant system. "Energy conditions": check which conditions a perfect fluid and a cosmological constant satisfy, and locate exactly which hypothesis of the singularity theorem a positive Lambda threatens.
units.checkpoint: You show that inside the Kerr ergosphere no timelike worldline can hold r, theta and phi constant, compute the Penrose process ceiling, and state the singularity theorem with its energy condition and name a matter content that violates it.

capstone:
**One orbit, six descriptions, and an error budget that must close.**

The sister course's capstone attacked one problem with four traditions and refereed them. This does the same to the two-body problem — the only system that appears in every part of this curriculum, and one with a century of published measurements to be wrong against.

Describe a gravitationally bound two-body system six ways, in increasing order of what the description costs.

1. **Newtonian** (00, 08). Closed ellipses, Kepler's laws, exact. What does this predict for Mercury's perihelion, and for the Hulse-Taylor binary's orbital period?
2. **Analytical** (11, 12, 13, 14, and 15 if you took it). The same orbits from the action; every conserved quantity produced from a symmetry by Noether, including Runge-Lenz; the whole problem in action-angle variables so the frequencies appear without the trajectory, and "precession" becomes the statement that two frequencies fail to be equal.
3. **Perturbative** (10, 21). The precession caused by the other planets — about 531 arcsec per century — computed by osculating elements and averaging, not looked up. This step is usually skipped, and it is the one that makes the classical test honest: without it the residual 43 is a number someone told you.
4. **Special-relativistic** (27). Relativistic kinematics with a 1/r potential. It precesses, and it gives roughly one sixth of the residual. State precisely why the answer is wrong: gravity is not a potential in Minkowski space.
5. **Schwarzschild geodesics** (36, 37). The full answer: 42.98 arcsec per century, 1.75 arcsec of deflection, the ISCO at six gravitational radii. Explain the extra -GML^2/c^2r^3 term geometrically, and trace the factor of two in the deflection to a named metric component.
6. **Radiative** (38, if taken). The system radiates. Quadrupole luminosity, orbital decay, inspiral time.

**Then confront the data.** Assemble the arcsecond budget for Mercury and defend every line: 5025 from the equinoxes, about 531 from Venus, Jupiter and the rest, about 0.03 from solar oblateness, 42.98 from general relativity, against 5600 observed. Do the same for light. Do the same for Hulse-Taylor's period derivative against -2.423 +/- 0.001 e-12. Integrate the Schwarzschild geodesics numerically as a cross-check on the perturbative answers, and report where the perturbation series stops being trustworthy.

**The deliverable** is a document in which each contribution is derived from stated principles, each approximation is named with its order, each number carries an uncertainty on both sides of the comparison, and the special-relativistic factor of six is confronted rather than skipped. Every number is computed by you; reference values appear only for comparison. If the error budget does not close to within the observational uncertainty, the capstone is not finished — and you will know precisely which term you got wrong. That failing-loudly property is this course's substitute for the sister course's solver benchmark: it is the assessment, not a decoration on it.

Estimated 20–25 h.
express_route: Twenty-four units, and unlike the two drafts this was synthesised from, it is genuinely closed: every unit on the route has all of its `needs` on the route. Nothing is bought with an apology in a footnote. It reaches the Einstein field equations, Schwarzschild, and Mercury's 43 arcseconds.
00 — Newton's second law as an ODE; quadrature; dimensional analysis
01 — determinism: Picard-Lindelof and Norton's dome
02 — phase portraits, Lyapunov functions, bifurcations
03 — curves, frames, the multivariable chain rule, Coriolis
04 — work: line integrals, gradient, curl, Stokes, the Poincare lemma
05 — flux: the divergence theorem, Poisson's equation, the tidal tensor
06 — the damped driven oscillator and linear ODE theory
08 — the central-force problem and the Binet equation
10 — multipoles, Legendre, and secular perturbation
11 — the calculus of variations, with conjugate points
12 — Lagrangian mechanics and coordinate invariance
13 — Noether's theorem
14 — Hamiltonian mechanics, the Legendre transform, Liouville
16 — rigid bodies, and what a tensor actually is
21 — perturbation theory and asymptotics
26 — Minkowski space and the Lorentz group
27 — relativistic dynamics and the proper-time action
30 — the equivalence principle and Rindler coordinates
31 — manifolds, tangent vectors, tensor fields
32 — metric, connection, geodesics, the Newtonian limit
33 — curvature and geodesic deviation
35 — the Einstein field equations (route two: Bianchi, Lovelock, Newtonian limit)
36 — Schwarzschild, Birkhoff, Kruskal
37 — the classical tests

WHAT THE ROUTE COSTS, NAMED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. Unit 26 derives the Lorentz group from homogeneity, isotropy and one invariant speed — which is honest mathematics — but the *value* of that speed is taken on credit, because unit 25 is what forces it out of Maxwell. You will believe relativity rather than having been cornered into it. Unit 35 gives you route two only: the field equations are shown to be the unique divergence-free second-order symmetric tensor by Bianchi and Lovelock, with the coupling fixed by the Newtonian limit — correct, complete, and silent on where the right-hand side comes from, which unit 29 is what answers. The stress tensor is restricted to dust, defined directly in unit 27's four-vector language; that is enough for 36 and 37 and not enough for 39.

WHAT ELSE YOU LOSE: the entire wave, Fourier, Sturm-Liouville, complex-analysis and electromagnetic apparatus (07, 09, 18, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, 25, 28, 29) — and with it the historical reason anyone believed relativity, Maxwell as the canonical tensor field, Cauchy's proof that stress is bilinear, and any route into 34, 38 or 39. About 195 hours against the full course's 335.

A SECOND ABBREVIATION, for a learner who wants the mathematics more than the physics: 00, 01, 02, 04, 06, 11, 18, 19, 20, 21, 31, 32, 33 — thirteen units ending at Riemannian geometry, which is a respectable graduate methods course in its own right. It is closed too, and it has no physics prerequisite beyond unit 00.
exclusions: **Quantum mechanics, in every form.** The largest exclusion and the most tempting to breach: by unit 19 you own Sturm-Liouville theory, separation of variables and L^2; by unit 15 you own Hamilton-Jacobi and the eikonal; by unit 21 you own WKB. The Schrodinger equation is about two hours away at three separate points. It is excluded because you named relativity as the destination and because quantum mechanics is not a topic one appends: it is a second course of comparable size. The seams are flagged in one sentence each — Poisson brackets becoming commutators in unit 14, the WKB limit in unit 21, Hawking temperature in unit 40 — and not pursued.

**Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics**, except the single adiabatic relation unit 22 needs for the speed of sound. The road from mechanics to relativity does not pass through entropy. Unit 14's Liouville theorem is where statistical mechanics would naturally begin, and the slide says so and stops. The cost is real: unit 40's black-hole thermodynamics has to be stated rather than understood.

**Quantum field theory and everything downstream.** Unit 29 deliberately builds classical field theory in the shape quantum field theory later uses, so this course is good preparation for it; the preparation is the whole of the contribution. The Unruh effect is gestured at by unit 30's Rindler horizon and Hawking radiation stated in unit 40, neither derived.

**Laboratory work, measurement technique and error analysis as disciplines**, per your request — honoured, with one qualification. Published measurements appear constantly (Pound-Rebka, Cassini, Hulse-Taylor, LIGO, Planck, MICROSCOPE, VLBI) *with their uncertainties*, because a prediction compared against a number with no error bar is not a test. You are asked to be right about nature, not to measure it.

**Fluid dynamics past the linear-acoustic level**: turbulence, boundary layers as a subject, vorticity dynamics, conformal-mapping aerofoils, the whole of aerodynamics. Unit 22 takes the stress tensor and the sound wave and stops. The dimensional-analysis lessons fluids teaches best — Reynolds number, Kolmogorov scaling, the boundary layer as a singular perturbation — are harvested into units 00 and 21 as problems, which is where their value for this destination actually lies.

**Optics as a subject.** Fermat's principle (unit 11), the eikonal limit (units 15 and 21), and dispersion (unit 20) are in because they are load-bearing. Lenses, interferometry, diffraction theory, Fresnel and Fraunhofer, coherence and imaging are out: a beautiful application of unit 19's Fourier analysis, and on no path to Einstein's equations.

**Circuits, AC analysis, electromagnetic media, transmission lines, antennas, waveguides and plasma physics** — the applied two-thirds of a standard electromagnetism course. Units 23 through 25 take Maxwell as far as radiation and then turn towards relativity, which is the only reason electromagnetism is here.

**Spinors, the Dirac equation, and the double cover SL(2,C) -> SO+(1,3).** A genuine gap in a relativity course, and the exclusion I am least comfortable with, since spinors are arguably the deepest thing special relativity contains. They are out because nothing on the road to the Schwarzschild tests requires them and adding them honestly costs two units.

**Gauge theory beyond the U(1) example in unit 29's second problem**: fibre bundles, connections on principal bundles, the tetrad formalism. Unit 34 goes as far as differential forms and Cartan's structure equations and stops.

**Numerical relativity, the ADM 3+1 split, and the Cauchy problem for Einstein's equations.** Named in units 35 and 38, taught in neither. A serious subject and a separate course — and the one that actually produces the waveform templates unit 38 compares against.
**Alternative theories of gravity**: Brans-Dicke, f(R), TeVeS and the rest. Unit 35's Lovelock argument is the right lens on the whole family, and it is one slide rather than a unit.

**Measure-theoretic rigour and functional analysis proper.** L^2 is used as an inner product space; completeness of eigenfunction systems is cited rather than proved; Lebesgue integration is named where it matters and never used; distributions are introduced operationally in unit 20. You have the maturity to prove these and would enjoy it, and it would cost three units that buy no physics.
**Numerical methods as a discipline** — discretisation, stability, stiffness, symplectic integrators, convergence order. Several problems end in arithmetic; none end in a library.

**History of science narrated for its own sake.** Dates, names and corrections to the received story appear throughout — Poincare's prize memoir in unit 17, the 1919 eclipse's actual error bars in unit 37 — but only where the history *is* the argument: Newton's isothermal sound speed, Maxwell's displacement current, Michelson-Morley, Le Verrier's missing planet.
reading: **Mechanics.** Landau & Lifshitz, *Mechanics* — 170 pages deriving all of classical mechanics from symmetry with zero padding, terse to the point of rudeness, and exactly right for a reader with maturity and no patience for drill. The primary text for Parts A and B. Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics* — the same material as geometry, and the book that makes units 14, 15 and 17 feel inevitable; read it alongside Landau, not instead. Spivak, *Physics for Mathematicians: Mechanics I* — written for precisely this learner and unusually honest about where the physics literature is sloppy; slow, and worth it for units 12 through 14. Goldstein, Poole & Safko — consulted when Landau is too compressed, particularly for rigid bodies.

**Problem sources for Parts A and B.** Morin, *Introduction to Classical Mechanics* — every problem has a full worked solution, which is exactly this course's format, so it is the model as well as the supply. Lim, *Problems and Solutions on Mechanics* and its electromagnetism and relativity companions — thousands of solved problems, the right raw material for a course whose every problem carries a solution.

**The analytic toolkit.** Teschl, *Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems* (free from the author) — units 01, 02, 06 and 17, with Picard-Lindelof at the right level of proof. Strogatz, *Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos* — unit 02's pictures, and the best-written book on this list. Hubbard & Hubbard, *Vector Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Differential Forms* — units 04, 05 and 34 in one volume, rigorous without austerity; Spivak's *Calculus on Manifolds* is the 140-page alternative and the proof of Stokes' theorem to own. Gelfand & Fomin, *Calculus of Variations* — unit 11, short, Dover-cheap, and including the conjugate-point theory most books omit. Strauss, *Partial Differential Equations* — unit 18, the cleanest treatment of classification and well-posedness at this level; Evans chapters 2-4 when you want more. Stein & Shakarchi, *Fourier Analysis* and *Complex Analysis* — units 19 and 20, two volumes of one series, which keeps notation consistent across the seam where the course needs both at once. Bender & Orszag, *Advanced Mathematical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* — unit 21, the only book that takes divergent series seriously and the source of several of its problems.

**Electromagnetism.** Griffiths, *Introduction to Electrodynamics* — units 23 and 24, the standard for good reason. Purcell & Morin, *Electricity and Magnetism* — the source of unit 28's wire-and-charge argument in its original form. Schwartz, *Principles of Electrodynamics* (Dover) — builds electromagnetism relativity-first, deriving magnetism from electrostatics plus a boost; unit 28's worked example written as a whole book. Zangwill when Griffiths is too brief; Jackson consulted, never read.

**Special relativity.** Taylor & Wheeler, *Spacetime Physics* (free PDF from the authors) — unit 26's geometric framing and the source of 'proper time is arc length'. Rindler, *Relativity: Special, General and Cosmological* — the group-theoretic derivation done carefully, and the best account of Born rigidity for unit 27.

**Geometry.** Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds* — unit 31's reference, and the book that makes 'a tensor is a multilinear map' stick; chapters 1-14 and 17. Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds* — unit 32, with the Levi-Civita uniqueness proof done properly; do Carmo is the shorter alternative. O'Neill, *Semi-Riemannian Geometry with Applications to Relativity* — the one geometry book written in indefinite signature from the start, and therefore the one that never has to apologise later; the ideal bridge from unit 33 to Part F. Frankel, *The Geometry of Physics* — spans units 04, 16, 31, 32 and 34 in one volume and connects them to the physics as it goes.

**General relativity.** Carroll, *Spacetime and Geometry* (lecture-note version free) — the main text for Part F, best on physical motivation and on getting to Schwarzschild quickly, and matching this course's (-,+,+,+) conventions. Wald, *General Relativity* — the rigorous account and the obvious second book for someone who writes proofs; chapters 1-6 track units 31-37 almost exactly, and 9-12 are where units 36 and 40 get their precision. Misner, Thorne & Wheeler, *Gravitation* — consulted rather than read, but unit 33's geodesic-deviation-versus-tidal-tensor comparison is theirs and is worth reading in the original. Hartle, *Gravity* — physics-first, useful as a second pass over unit 37's tests. Zee, *Einstein Gravity in a Nutshell* — unit 35's Einstein-Hilbert variation, done more readably than anyone. Poisson, *A Relativist's Toolkit* — unit 35's boundary term and unit 40's horizons and surface gravity. Maggiore, *Gravitational Waves, Volume 1* — unit 38. Weinberg, *Gravitation and Cosmology* — unit 39, and worth an afternoon as the dissenting view that deliberately downplays geometry.

**Problem source for Parts D, E and F.** Lightman, Press, Price & Teukolsky, *Problem Book in Relativity and Gravitation* — 475 problems with complete worked solutions. For units 26 through 40 this is not a supplement; it is the problem sets.
open_questions: **How much electromagnetism — and this is the biggest sizing decision left.** This proposal commits three spine units before relativity (23 static fields, 24 Maxwell, 25 the crisis) plus two after (28 the field tensor, 29 field theory), roughly 32 hours, on four grounds: it is the only place vector calculus reaches its final form, since Stokes' theorem does no real work until Ampere's law; it is what makes the invariance of c a conclusion rather than a decree, which matters more for you than for most learners; F_{mu nu} is the canonical tensor field and makes unit 33's index work routine rather than alarming; and its stress-energy tensor is a standard source. I merged electrostatics and magnetostatics into one unit because unit 19 already gave you Legendre, Bessel and Green's functions, so most of electrostatics is transfer rather than new content — one of the two drafts spent two units there and I judged that bloat. The alternative is one unit that states Maxwell and moves on, saving about 25 hours and turning relativity into a postulate you accepted. Your call changes units 23-25, 28, 29 and 38.

**Should differential forms (34) be spine rather than branch?** One draft made forms the *first* treatment of vector calculus, at unit 05, specialising down to grad/div/curl. I rejected that: teaching flux as a 2-form to someone who has never computed a flux produces a learner who can prove d^2 = 0 and cannot guess which way a field points, which is the exact failure mode this course is designed against. But the reverse case is real — Maxwell as dF = 0, gauge freedom as exactness, the solenoid as a de Rham class, and Cartan's structure equations making every curvature computation about four times shorter. It is a branch here because nothing on the spine strictly needs it. If you take it, take it *immediately after* unit 33 rather than at the end, and accept a translation tax on every textbook page, since every book in the reading list computes curvature in coordinates.

**Should the field equations be derived or postulated?** Unit 35 currently offers both routes and unit 29 (classical field theory) is spine so that the full course does the derivation. Route two — Bianchi plus Lovelock plus the Newtonian limit — is complete, forced, and silent about where T^{mu nu} comes from. Route one costs unit 29 and answers exactly the question a mathematician asks first. I kept both and made 35 need only route two's prerequisites, which is what lets the express route be genuinely closed. If you never intend to take the express route, 29 could become a formal prerequisite of 35 and the unit would be cleaner.

**Signature convention.** (-,+,+,+) throughout, matching Carroll, Wald, MTW, O'Neill and Weinberg; the particle-physics literature uses (+,-,-,-), and unit 27's Mandelstam invariants are conventionally written there. Whichever you choose must be chosen once and printed on every slide: a sign error at unit 32 propagates silently to unit 37 and surfaces as a wrong number for Mercury, which is the worst possible place to discover it.

**Does any of this get formalised?** You write Lean and Rocq, and four things here are tractable: Picard-Lindelof (unit 01, mathlib already has the uniqueness theorem), the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (11), the uniqueness of the Levi-Civita connection (32), and the Riemann tensor's symmetries and component count (33). Formalising any of them would give this course what the sister course's solver comparisons gave it — an external referee that does not care how convincing the argument felt. It would also be a substantial detour. Worth deciding before unit 01 is built rather than after.

**Where the worked solutions live.** Every problem needs a full solution plus a hint ladder, which is a large amount of LaTeX-heavy prose. The sister course settled on one Org file per unit with `#+startup: content` after discovering that HTML `<details>` folds only in a browser and Emacs showed every rung open. The same shape would work, but heavy mathematics renders badly in Org's LaTeX fragments. The alternatives are a compiled PDF per unit (typesets best, folds worst) and a second reveal.js deck per unit revealed one rung at a time (native hint ladder, worst to write). Settle this before unit 00 is built; retrofitting forty units of mathematics into a different format is exactly the work nobody does.

**The size, and what to cut first.** Forty-one units at 6–10.5 h is about 335 hours, against the sister course's 155, because this one teaches five separate mathematical subjects on the way through. The express route reaches Mercury's 43 arcseconds in 24 units and about 195 hours. If the full course is too long, cut in this order: unit 17 (chaos) first, since it feeds only branch 40 and is a genuine detour from the Newton-to-Einstein line; then unit 40, since it depends on branch 15 and a chain of two branches is a lot of machinery for one payoff; then unit 09 (Kepler's equation and Bessel), accepting that unit 19's drum must then take Bessel on trust and unit 20 loses its best debt to pay off.

**Things I judged and deliberately did not fix.** (a) Unit 02 (phase portraits) feeds almost nothing downstream and stays on the spine purely because it is the best intuition-builder in the course for someone who is fluent in proof and blank on physics — that is a pedagogical bet, not a structural necessity, and you may disagree. (b) Unit 19 merges Fourier series and Sturm-Liouville into a 10.5-hour unit, the largest here; splitting it is defensible and would take the count to 42. (c) Units 15 and 17 both exist partly for pleasure, and I have said so rather than dressing them up as prerequisites. (d) A quantum coda — non-relativistic quantum mechanics as spectral theory, then Dirac — would fit naturally after unit 21 and is excluded only because you did not ask; say the word and it reopens. (e) Spinors remain the exclusion I am least comfortable with.
